dervis-irab:73-76.t:
* Vocabulary:
(مَقاماً): with fatḥa on the mīm, a noun of place from قام, or a mīmī maṣdar (verbal noun with prefixed mīm). It was also read مُقاما with ḍamma, in which case it is likewise a noun of place or a mīmī maṣdar from the augmented four-letter verb أقام. What is meant here is the place where people stay.
(نَدِيًّا): الندي is the assembly, the gathering place of a people where they meet together (ينتدون); one also says النادي.
(أَثاثاً): الأثاث is household furnishings and wealth. One says أثّ يئث ويأث ويؤث أثاثا وأثوثا وأثاثة of plants or hair: it became dense and abundant, so it is أث and أثيث.
(رِءْياً): of the pattern فِعْل in the sense of مفعول, meaning "appearance, sight"; it is like الطحن and الذبح in the sense of المطحون (what is ground) and المذبوح (what is slaughtered). It is from رأيت with metathesis, as in their saying راء for رأى; or from الري, which is comfort and luxury, from their saying ريان النعيم ("saturated with comfort").

* I'rab:
(وَإِذا تُتْلى عَلَيْهِمْ آياتُنا بَيِّناتٍ قالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا): the wāw is resumptive (istiʾnāfiyya) and إذا is a conditional for the future; the clause تتلى is in the genitive construct with the adverb (ẓarf); عليهم is attached to (mutaʿalliq) تتلى; آياتنا is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent); بينات is a ḥāl (circumstantial) of آياتنا, i.e. clear, making plain their aims and meanings. The clause قال الذين كفروا has no grammatical position because it is the apodosis (jawāb).
(لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَيُّ الْفَرِيقَيْنِ خَيْرٌ مَقاماً وَأَحْسَنُ نَدِيًّا): للذين آمنوا is attached to قال, and the clause آمنوا is the ṣila (relative clause). أي is interrogative, the mubtadaʾ (subject); خير is the khabar (predicate); مقاما is a tamyīz (specification); أحسن is conjoined to خير; and نديا is a tamyīz.
(وَكَمْ أَهْلَكْنا قَبْلَهُمْ مِنْ قَرْنٍ هُمْ أَحْسَنُ أَثاثاً وَرِءْياً): كم is the declarative (khabariyya) kam, in the position of the accusative as the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) of أهلكنا; أهلكنا is a verb and its agent; من قرن is a non-explicit tamyīz of كم, because the tamyīz of declarative كم is often made genitive by من — the details of this will come later. هم is a mubtadaʾ and أحسن its khabar, and the clause is in the position of the accusative as an adjective (ṣifa) of declarative كم. Do you not see that if you dropped هم you would have no choice but to put أحسن in the accusative as an adjective? This is what al-Zamakhsharī mentioned, and Abū al-Baqāʾ followed him in taking هم أحسن as an adjective of كم; but our colleagues have stated explicitly that interrogative and declarative كم are neither qualified by an adjective nor used as one. أثاثا is a tamyīz and رئيا is conjoined to it. It is also possible for it [Translator's note: the clause هم أحسن] to be an adjective of قرن.
(قُلْ مَنْ كانَ فِي الضَّلالَةِ فَلْيَمْدُدْ لَهُ الرَّحْمنُ مَدًّا): من is a conditional noun that puts the verb in the jussive, a mubtadaʾ; كان is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ), a defective (nāqiṣ) past verb, its noun latent (mustatir) referring to من, and في الضلالة is the khabar of كان. The fāʾ links the apodosis; the lām is the lām of command; يمدد is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by the lām of command; له is attached to يمدد; الرحمن is the fāʿil (agent); and مدا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object).
(حَتَّى إِذا رَأَوْا ما يُوعَدُونَ إِمَّا الْعَذابَ وَإِمَّا السَّاعَةَ): حتى is a particle of limit and of the genitive, attached to the apodosis, which is فسيعلمون. It was also said that it is inceptive, i.e. clauses begin after it. al-Shihāb said in his gloss on al-Bayḍāwī: "حتى here is an inceptive particle, i.e. clauses begin after it, i.e. are begun anew; so it is neither a genitive-governing particle nor a conjunction — and likewise wherever it comes before conditional إذا." The clause رأوا is in the genitive construct with the adverb; ما is a mafʿūl bihi; the clause يوعدون is the ṣila; إما is a particle of condition and detailing; and العذاب and الساعة are a badal (substitute) of ما. The meaning: they continue in their transgression until they come to know, when they see the punishment or the Hour, who is worse in position and weaker in forces.
(فَسَيَعْلَمُونَ مَنْ هُوَ شَرٌّ مَكاناً وَأَضْعَفُ جُنْداً): the fāʾ falls in the apodosis of إذا — and this is what favours taking إذا [Translator's note: so in the source; the argument concerns حتى] as being for limit. سيعلمون is an imperfect verb in the nominative (marfūʿ), and the wāw is the agent. من is a relative noun, the mafʿūl bihi; هو is a mubtadaʾ and شر its khabar, and the clause is the ṣila. It is also possible that من is interrogative, in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ, with هو a second mubtadaʾ and شر the khabar of the second mubtadaʾ; هو with its khabar is the khabar of من. In that case the clause suspends (muʿallaqa) the verb of perception, so the clause is in the position of the accusative as the object of يعلمون.
(وَيَزِيدُ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ اهْتَدَوْا هُدىً): you may take the wāw as resumptive, so the clause is a new start; or you may take it as a conjunction, conjoining the clause to the conditional clause reported by the verb of saying, i.e. "and say: Allah increases…". يزيد الله الذين اهتدوا is an imperfect verb, its agent and its object; the clause اهتدوا is the ṣila; and هدى is a tamyīz or a second object of يزيد.
(وَالْباقِياتُ الصَّالِحاتُ خَيْرٌ عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ ثَواباً وَخَيْرٌ مَرَدًّا): الباقيات is a mubtadaʾ and الصالحات an adjective; خير is the khabar of الباقيات; the adverb عند ربك is attached to خير; ثوابا is a tamyīz; and خير مردا is conjoined to خير ثوابا, i.e. [better] in return, outcome and consequence.

* Benefits:
1- The من that comes before the tamyīz:
There is disagreement about the meaning of the من that is stated explicitly with the tamyīz. It was said that it is partitive (li-l-tabʿīḍ), and for this reason it does not occur in expressions like طاب نفسا, because نفسا is not more general than the vague element contained in the clause. al-Shalawbīn said: it is redundant (zāʾida) according to Sībawayh, for the sense of partition; and what shows this to be correct is that a word was conjoined in the accusative to its [underlying] position. al-Ḥuṭayʾa said:
طافت أمامة بالركبان آونة ... يا حسنه من قوام ما ومنتقبا
(Umāma went round with the riders at times — how beautiful he was in stature, and veiled!)
أمامة, with ḍamma on the hamza, is a woman's name; آونة, with madd, is accusative as an adverb. The point of evidence is in his saying من قوام: it is a tamyīz made genitive by redundant من in an affirmative statement, and for this reason منتقبا was conjoined to its position in the accusative; ما is redundant for emphasis of the statement. Ibn Hishām said that it is for explaining the genus (li-bayān al-jins), and al-Zamakhsharī preceded him in this, because the well-known view of the grammarians other than al-Akhfash is that من is redundant only in non-affirmative statements.

2- The meaning of the comparative:
It was asked: what is the meaning of the comparative in His saying «وَالْباقِياتُ الصَّالِحاتُ خَيْرٌ عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ ثَواباً وَخَيْرٌ مَرَدًّا»? Is there any doubt [about it]? And do those who boast have any share in the reward and the outcome? Two answers were given. The first is that it is from their concise speech: they say "summer is hotter than winter", i.e. more extreme in its heat than winter is in its cold. The second is that the comparative noun is mentioned by way of mushākala (stylistic correspondence) with their earlier speech. al-Shihāb said in his gloss on al-Bayḍāwī: "This is an answer to what was imagined: how could [the believers] be preferred over them in the goodness of reward and outcome, when the comparative requires sharing, while they have no reward and their outcome has no good in it?"

dervis-irab:77-84.t:
* Vocabulary:
(أَطَّلَعَ): its origin is أاطلع; the connecting hamza (hamzat al-waṣl) was dropped and the interrogative hamza with fatḥa remained. اطلع is transitive by itself and by means of a preposition: one says اطلع الأمر and اطلع عليه, meaning "he came to know it". One also says اطّلع طِلْعَ العدو, with kasra on the ṭāʾ and sukūn on the lām: he learned the inner state of their affairs. Some imagined that it is transitive only with على, and so parsed الغيب as accusative by removal of the preposition (manṣūb bi-nazʿ al-khāfiḍ); but it is in fact from their saying اطلع الجبل when one climbs to its summit, and طلع الثنية (he climbed the mountain pass). Jarīr said:
إني إذا مضر عليّ تحدثت ... لاقيت مطلع الجبال وعورا
(When Muḍar talk against me, I meet the ascents of the mountains as rugged places.)
مطلع is a noun of place from the doubled اطّلع, whose origin is اطتلع on the pattern iftiʿāl; the tāʾ was changed to ṭāʾ and assimilated into what precedes it. In the verse it is accusative as an adverb, and الوعور, the plural of وعر (difficult), is the object of لاقيت; or مطلع is the object and وعورا a ḥāl (circumstantial). He is saying: when Muḍar fabricate against me what I do not accept, or their souls whisper to them to kill me, I grapple with hardships and pay them no heed. Further discussion of its use in the verse will come in the section on Rhetoric.
(وَنَمُدُّ): imperfect of مدّ الشيء يمده, of the نصر pattern: to lengthen it, spread it out and pull it. مدّ الحبل فامتدّ (he stretched the rope and it extended), and هذا ممدّ الحبل (this is where the rope is stretched). Ibn Muqbil said:
وللشمس أسباب كأن شعاعها ... ممدّ حبال في خباء مطنّب
(The sun has cords, as though its rays were ropes stretched across a tent fastened with guy-ropes.)
And تمدّد الأديم (the hide stretched), طراف ممدّد (an extended leather tent), and أمد الجيش وضم إليه ألف رجل مددا (he reinforced the army, adding to it a thousand men as reinforcement). The mīm with the dāl in particular carries the sense of extension, as though the root of the material embraces other derived forms; and this is among the distinctive features of our immortal Arabic language. One says مدحه and امتدحه: he lengthened his praise of him; مدخ فلانا, with the dotted khāʾ: he supported him with help, whether his deed was good or bad; and تمدخ: he was proud and arrogant — and it is not hidden how much extension and inflation there is in pride and arrogance. مدر المكان: he reached the place and extended to it; مدر الحوض: he sealed the gaps between the stones of the basin with مدر, which is sticky clay unmixed with sand that spreads quickly when you plaster a wall with it or smooth it. مدس الجلد ونحوه: he rubbed the hide and the like so that it would stretch. مدشت عينه: darkness spread over it and its nerve became slack; مدشت يده: his hand became thin and small, so that it appeared to the onlooker stretched out because of the little flesh on it. المدش, with two fatḥas, is darkness that spreads over the eye from hunger, and the slackness of the nerves of the hand. تمدل بالمنديل: he tied the cloth on his head or wrapped it as a turban — which is close to the meaning of extension. مدّن المدائن: he built cities, founded them as towns and renewed their building, so they extended in breadth and length; المدينة is a cluster of houses that grew and extended, and so it was called a "city". From this, the city at Yathrib was named [al-Madīna], and Madīnat al-Salām, i.e. Baghdad; and al-Madāʾin is a city near Baghdad in which was the Īwān of Chosroes, called by the plural because of its size and extent. About it al-Buḥturī composed his poem rhyming in sīn, referring to it in his saying: حضرت رحلي الهموم فوجهت إلى أبيض المدائن عنسي (Cares came to my saddle, so I turned my strong she-camel towards the White Palace of al-Madāʾin.)
أتسلى عن الهموم وآسى ... لمحلّ من آل ساسان درس
(To console myself from cares, and to grieve for an effaced dwelling of the house of Sāsān.)
And مدهه, i.e. he praised him, as already mentioned. المدى is the long, extended limit; أمدى فلانا and ماداه: he granted him respite; أمدى الرجل: the man advanced in age, and it extended; تمادى في غيه: he persisted in his deed and went on extending in his wickedness [Translator's note: the source has عيه; read as غيه]. المدية, with ḍamma on the mīm, is the large, long blade. This is among the wonders of our noble language.
(وَنَرِثُهُ): i.e. We strip him of it and take it, by bringing him out of the world empty of that; what is meant is that We withhold from him what he says he will obtain in the Hereafter.
(تَؤُزُّهُمْ): الأز is provoking, stirring up and violent agitation. This is among the most remarkable roots of the Arabic language: all of them indicate this meaning. الأز is also the intensity of sound, and from it أز المرجل أزا وأزيزا: the cauldron boiled and its boiling became intense until a sound was heard from it. In the ḥadīth: «فكان له أزيز» ("and there was a seething sound from him"). In al-Qāmūs: "أزّت القدر تؤز, with ḍamma, and تئز, with kasra, أزا وأزيزا وأزازا, with fatḥa: its boiling became intense; أز النار: he kindled the fire; أز الشيء: he moved it violently." In al-Lisān, al-Asās and others:
"The rumbling (أزيز) of the thunder frightened me, and the grinding (أزيز) of the millstone and its rattling split my head"; أزه على كذا: he incited him to it and pushed him to it with agitation; هو يأتز من كذا: he is irritated and disturbed by it; تأزر المجلس: the gathering stirred up those in it. All of this indicates movement and agitation. And أزب الماء يأزب, with ḍamma and kasra: the water flowed rapidly, and الميزاب is the water spout, plural مآزيب; أزج البيت: he built the house in length and breadth; أزحت قدمه: his foot slipped; أزر يأزر, with kasra, بالشيء: he surrounded it, and of plants: they became dense; آزره مؤازرة: he helped him and hastened to his aid; الأزر is strength and the back — one says شد به أزره, i.e. his back; المئزر is well known, and one says شد للأمر مئزره when someone rolls up his sleeves for something and hurries to it. أزف يأزف, with fatḥa, أزفا وأزوفا: it drew near; أزف الرجل: the man hurried; آزفه إيزافا: he hurried him [Translator's note: the source has إنزافا]; أزفت الآزفة: the Resurrection drew near; فلان يمشي الأزفى, with three vowels: he walks fast. المأزق is a narrow place and the place of battle; أزل يأزل: he fell into straits and hardship; أزمه أزما وأزوما: he bit him; [أزم] الحبل: he twisted the rope tightly; تأزم القوم: a crisis befell the people; الأزمة, with fatḥa on the hamza and sukūn on the zāy, and الآزمة are hardship and straits; أزمى الرجل: he was level with him and near him, and sat إزاءه, i.e. in front of him. In all of this there is what indicates movement; the letter zāy in general indicates this or what is close to it, and you will come across marvellous things about its peculiar nature.
(وَوَلَداً): الولد is a singular noun standing in place of the plural. الوُلْد, with ḍamma on the wāw and sukūn — and it has been read so — means the same as الولد, so they are two dialectal forms; it was also said that it is rather the plural of ولد, like أسد and أُسْد, عرب and عُرْب.

* I'rab:
(أَفَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي كَفَرَ بِآياتِنا وَقالَ لَأُوتَيَنَّ مالًا وَوَلَداً): the hamza is for the interrogative of wonder, and the fāʾ keeps its sense of sequence, as if He said: I will also tell you the story of this unbeliever following the account of those. رأيت here means "tell me", and it has been discussed in detail earlier. الذي is its first object; the clause كفر بآياتنا is the ṣila (relative clause); قال is conjoined to كفر. لأوتين: the lām is the answer to an implied oath; the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) is a hidden pronoun, its implied form being "I"; مالا is the second object of أوتين; and ولدا is conjoined to مالا.
(أَطَّلَعَ الْغَيْبَ أَمِ اتَّخَذَ عِنْدَ الرَّحْمنِ عَهْداً): the hamza is interrogative; اطلع is a past verb, and its fāʿil (agent) is "he", referring to the unbeliever — said to be al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil; his story will come in the section on Benefits. أم is a conjunction corresponding to the hamza; اتخذ is a past verb whose agent is latent (mustatir), referring to him; عند الرحمن is the second object of اتخذ; and عهدا the first object.
(كَلَّا سَنَكْتُبُ ما يَقُولُ وَنَمُدُّ لَهُ مِنَ الْعَذابِ مَدًّا): كلا is a particle of deterrence and rebuke, about which there are many views that we shall present in the section on Benefits. سنكتب is an imperfect verb in the nominative (marfūʿ), its agent latent, its implied form being "We". He prefixed it with sīn after the manner of what one who threatens says to his opponent, "I will take revenge on you", meaning: do not be deceived by the length of time, for revenge is coming to you; or [it means] We will show him and let him know that We have written. ما is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object) and the clause يقول is the ṣila. نمد is conjoined to نكتب; له is attached to (mutaʿalliq) نمد; من العذاب is a ḥāl (circumstantial), because it was [originally] an adjective of مدا; and مدا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object), or a direct object if it is in the sense of المدد (reinforcement).
(وَنَرِثُهُ ما يَقُولُ وَيَأْتِينا فَرْداً): نرثه is conjoined to نمد; the agent is "We"; the hāʾ is accusative by removal of the preposition; and ما is the direct object, the implied form being "and We shall inherit from him what he says". It is also possible that the hāʾ is the direct object and ما a badal ishtimāl (substitute of inclusion) of the hāʾ; the meaning is: We shall inherit what he has of wealth, family and children. The clause يقول is the ṣila. يأتينا is conjoined to what precedes; its agent is latent, its implied form being "he"; and نا is a "separating pronoun, agent" [Translator's note: so in the source (ضمير فصل فاعل); نا here is in fact an attached pronoun in the position of the object]. فردا is a ḥāl.
(وَاتَّخَذُوا مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ آلِهَةً لِيَكُونُوا لَهُمْ عِزًّا): اتخذوا is a verb and its agent; the first object is omitted, namely the idols understood from the context of the discourse; من دون الله is a ḥāl; and آلهة is the second object. ليكونوا: the lām is the lām of cause (taʿlīl); يكونوا is a defective imperfect verb in the accusative by an implied أن after the lām; the wāw is its noun; لهم is a ḥāl; and عزا is the khabar (predicate) of يكونوا.
(كَلَّا سَيَكْفُرُونَ بِعِبادَتِهِمْ وَيَكُونُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ ضِدًّا): كلا, as already stated, is a particle of deterrence and rebuke against their seeking might through them. سيكفرون is an imperfect verb in the nominative, and بعبادتهم is attached to يكفرون, i.e. they will deny their worship and disown it; so the maṣdar (verbal noun) is annexed to its object. يكونون is conjoined to يكفرون; the wāw is its noun; عليهم is a ḥāl; and ضدا is the khabar of يكونون. He made it singular although they are plural, in view of its origin, because it was originally a maṣdar and maṣdars are neither dualized nor pluralized; or because it is a singular with a plural meaning. al-Zamakhsharī has fine words on the singular form of الضد, which we will quote in the section on Rhetoric.
(أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّا أَرْسَلْنَا الشَّياطِينَ عَلَى الْكافِرِينَ تَؤُزُّهُمْ أَزًّا):
ألم: the hamza is for the interrogative of affirmation (taqrīr); لم is a particle of negation, conversion [to the past] and jussive; تر is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by لم, and its agent is "you". أن and what falls within its scope stand in place of the two objects of تر. أن, its noun, and the clause أرسلنا as its khabar; الشياطين is a direct object; the clause تؤزهم is a ḥāl; and أزا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq.
(فَلا تَعْجَلْ عَلَيْهِمْ إِنَّما نَعُدُّ لَهُمْ عَدًّا): the fāʾ is the faṣīḥa (the fāʾ indicating an implied condition), i.e. if you have understood all this, then do not hasten; عليهم is attached to تعجل; إنما is the restraining [mā] and the restrained [inna] (kāffa wa-makfūfa); the clause نعد لهم is a ḥāl; and عدا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq.

* Rhetoric:
1- The implied metaphor (al-istiʿāra al-makniyya):
1- The implied metaphor in His saying «اطلع الغيب»: the unknown Unseen, veiled in secrets, is likened to a lofty-peaked mountain to whose height no bird can climb; it is unknown, and upon it are dashed the hopes of those who wish to glimpse its horizons and grasp its terrors. Then the mountain, i.e. the thing to which it is likened, is omitted, and something of its properties and concomitants is taken, namely climbing, ascending and looking out upon what it conceals. The purpose of this metaphor is utter mockery, as if He were saying: has this one, with his baseness, his triviality and the smallness of his worth, reached the point of climbing up to the Unseen that is screened by secrets and sealed in concealment?

2- The singular form of الضد:
al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: why is it made singular? I say: it is made singular like the singular in his saying ﷺ «وهم يد على من سواهم» ('and they are one hand against those besides them'), because their word is united and they are like one thing through the excess of their solidarity and agreement." The wāw in يكفرون may refer to the gods, i.e. they will deny their [the idolaters'] worship of them; or to the idolaters, i.e. they will disown it because of the evil consequence and end.

* Benefits:
The aspects of كلّا:
The grammarians have six views on this word:
1- The view of the majority of the Basrans, such as al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash and Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Mubarrad, is that it is a particle of deterrence and rebuke; this meaning suits it wherever it occurs in the Noble Qur'an. Lovers have rebuked their censurers with it; one of them — most probably ʿUrwa ibn Udhayna — said:
يقلن لقد بكيت فقلت: كلّا ... وهل يبكي من الطرب الجليد؟
ولكن أصاب سواد عيني ... عويد قذى له طرف حديد
فقلن فما لدمعهما سواء ... أكلتا مقلتيك أصاب عود؟
(They said: "You have wept." I said: "Not at all! Does the steadfast one weep from emotion? But a little splinter of mote with a sharp tip struck the black of my eye." They said: "Then why do both your eyes shed tears alike — did a splinter strike both your eyes?")
2- The view of al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl is that it is a particle of affirmation meaning "yes", so it is an answer, and in that case something must precede it, either in wording or by implication.
3- The view of al-Kisāʾī, Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī, Naṣr ibn Yūsuf and Ibn Wāṣil is that it means "truly" (ḥaqqan).
4- The view of Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Bāhilī is that it is a rejection of what precedes it; this is close to the first.
5- That it is a connective (ṣila) in speech meaning إي — so it was said, but this is doubtful, since إي is an answer particle restricted to oaths.
6- That it is an opening particle (ḥarf istiftāḥ); this is the view of Abū Ḥātim.
كلا is mentioned in fifteen Meccan surahs, and the total number of times it is mentioned is thirty-three.

dervis-irab:85-98.t:
* Vocabulary:
(وَفْداً): الوفد is the maṣdar (verbal noun) of وفد يفد وفدا ووفودا ووفادة وإفادة.
[وفد] إلى or على the ruler: he came to him and arrived as an envoy, so he is وافد. [وفد is also] the plural of وافد: a group of people who gather together, come to a land and present themselves before the ruler and the like.
(وِرْداً): the people who come down to water thirsty, their necks almost severed by thirst.
(إِدًّا): with kasra and with fatḥa: something astonishing; it was also said: something enormous and abhorrent, and [it means] severity [Translator's note: the source reads ولادة الشدة, which appears corrupt]. آدني الأمر: the matter weighed on me and was grievous to me, إدا. In al-Qāmūs: "الإد and الإدة, both with kasra, are something astonishing, a hideous matter, a calamity and something abhorrent, like الأد with fatḥa; أدته الداهية تؤده, with ḍamma, تئده, with kasra, and تأده, with fatḥa: the calamity befell him."
(وُدًّا): affection and love. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "وددته أوده, of the تعب pattern, ودّا, with fatḥa and ḍamma on the wāw: I loved him [Translator's note: the source has أجببته, a misprint for أحببته]; the noun is المودة. And وددت لو كان كذا, also ودا and ودادة: I wished for it." In al-Mukhtār: "الود, with ḍamma, fatḥa and kasra on the wāw, is love; it has all three vowels on the wāw, the preferred being ḍamma, with which the Seven read; outside the Seven it was read with fatḥa and kasra. It is possible that the form with fatḥa is a maṣdar and those with ḍamma and kasra are nouns."
(لُدًّا): plural of ألد, i.e. very contentious. Fine is al-Zamakhsharī's statement:
"اللد are those severe and contentious with falsehood, who go into every لديد, i.e. every side of wrangling and disputation, through the excess of their obstinacy." In al-Asās: "a man is ألد, ألندد and يلندد, and there is لدد in him; people are لدّ; he disputed with him (لادّه) ملادة and لدادا, and he is fierce in disputing; I left so-and-so يتردد and يتلدد, turning about; he struck him on the لديدان of his neck, which are its two sides; and he struck him on his متلدّد, on his neck." He said:
ولو شئت نجتني من القوم جسرة ... بعيدة بين العجب والمتلدّد
(Had I wished, a bold she-camel would have rescued me from the people, broad between the base of the tail and the side of the neck.)
(رِكْزاً): الركز is a faint sound; from it ركز الرمح, when one plants the end of the spear in the ground; and الركاز is buried wealth.
And (تُحِسُّ): with ḍamma on the tāʾ, the imperfect of أحسّ. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "الحس and الحسيس are a faint sound; حسه حسا, so he is حسيس, like قتله قتلا, so he is قتيل; أحس الرجل الشيء إحساسا: he became aware of it; it is transitive by itself with the alif. The Exalted said: «فَلَمَّا أَحَسَّ عِيسى مِنْهُمُ الْكُفْرَ». Sometimes bāʾ is added to it, and one says أحس به in the sense of 'he sensed it'. And حسست به, of the قتل pattern, is a dialectal form of it; the maṣdar is الحس, with kasra; it is transitive with bāʾ, also in the sense of 'I sensed'."

* I'rab:
(يَوْمَ نَحْشُرُ الْمُتَّقِينَ إِلَى الرَّحْمنِ وَفْداً): the adverb (ẓarf) is accusative by an omitted verb, which some estimated as اذكر ("remember"), and al-Zamakhsharī estimated it with his saying: "يوم is accusative by something implied, i.e. on the day We gather and drive [them], We will do with the two groups what no description can encompass." Others said that what governs it is His later saying «لا يملكون». The clause نحشر is in the genitive construct with the adverb; the fāʿil (agent) of نحشر is a latent (mustatir) pronoun, its implied form being "We"; المتقين is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); إلى الرحمن is attached to (mutaʿalliq) نحشر; and وفدا is a ḥāl (circumstantial). The name الرحمن is repeated in this surah sixteen times.
(وَنَسُوقُ الْمُجْرِمِينَ إِلى جَهَنَّمَ وِرْداً): conjoined to the previous clause; وردا is also a ḥāl, i.e. coming down [to it], as thirsty people come down to water [Translator's note: the source has إليهم], on foot and thirsty, thirst all but killing them.
(لا يَمْلِكُونَ الشَّفاعَةَ إِلَّا مَنِ اتَّخَذَ عِنْدَ الرَّحْمنِ عَهْداً): the clause is resumptive (mustaʾnafa), brought to establish the state of all people, believers and unbelievers, and has no connection with the two groups mentioned before. لا is negating; يملكون is an imperfect verb in the nominative (marfūʿ); the wāw is the agent, referring to all people; الشفاعة is the direct object; إلا is a particle of restriction (ḥaṣr); and من is a relative noun whose position is nominative as a badal (substitute) of the wāw, or accusative as a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil). The clause اتخذ is the ṣila (relative clause); عند الرحمن is an adverb attached to an omitted element which is the second object of اتخذ; and عهدا is the first object. Abū al-Baqāʾ and al-Zamakhsharī preferred that the exception be disconnected (munqaṭiʿ). The views on this verse are confused, and for this reason we shall devote a special discussion to it in the section on Benefits.
(وَقالُوا اتَّخَذَ الرَّحْمنُ وَلَداً): the clause اتخذ الرحمن ولدا is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl); اتخذ الرحمن ولدا is a verb, its agent and its object.
(لَقَدْ جِئْتُمْ شَيْئاً إِدًّا): the lām prepares for the oath (muwaṭṭiʾa li-l-qasam); قد is a particle of realization (taḥqīq); جئتم is a verb and its agent; شيئا is a direct object; and إدا is an adjective.
(تَكادُ السَّماواتُ يَتَفَطَّرْنَ مِنْهُ وَتَنْشَقُّ الْأَرْضُ وَتَخِرُّ الْجِبالُ هَدًّا): تكاد is one of the verbs of approximation that operate like kāna; السموات is its noun; the clause يتفطرن is its khabar (predicate), the nūn being the agent; منه, a preposition and its genitive noun, is attached to يتفطرن. تنشق الأرض is an imperfect verb and its agent; تخر الجبال is an imperfect verb and its agent; and هدا is a maṣdar in the place of a ḥāl, i.e. demolished; or a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object), because it is a maṣdar not of the wording of the verb but synonymous with it, since الخرور is falling and collapse. al-Zamakhsharī also chose that it be a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), i.e. "because it is demolished". هدّ is used both transitively and intransitively: on the first view it is transitive, because the sense of the passive participle has been formed from it; on the second it is intransitive, because خر is intransitive and its synonym must be like it. Reflect on this, for it is subtle.
(أَنْ دَعَوْا لِلرَّحْمنِ وَلَداً): أن and what falls within its scope is a maṣdar about which there are three views. [First,] that it is a badal of the hāʾ in منه, so it is like his saying:
على حالة لو أن في القوم حاتما ... على جوده لضنّ بالماء حاتم
(In such a state that, were Ḥātim among the people, for all his generosity Ḥātim would have been stingy with the water.)
for حاتم has been transmitted in the genitive, because it is a badal of the pronoun in جوده; we shall discuss this verse in the section on Benefits. [Second,] the accusative by removal of the preposition, the preposition and its genitive noun being in the position of the accusative as a mafʿūl li-ajlihi: the demolishing is explained as caused by their ascribing a son to the All-Merciful. [Third,] the nominative as the agent of هدا, i.e. their ascribing a son to the All-Merciful demolished them.
دعوا is a past verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on an implied fatḥa on the alif that was dropped because of the meeting of two sukūns; للرحمن is attached to دعوا; ولدا is the second object of دعوا, and the first is omitted, its implied form being "their object of worship", because دعوا means "they named", which takes two objects; bāʾ may come before the second: you say دعوت ولدي بزيد and دعوت ولدي زيدا. The poet said:
دعتني أخاها أم عمرو ولم أكن ... أخاها ولم أرضع لها بلبان
(Umm ʿAmr called me her brother, though I was not her brother, nor did I suckle with her from one breast.)
Another said:
ألا رب من يدعى نصيحا وإن يغب تجده بغيب منك غير نصيح
(Many a one is called a sincere adviser, yet if he is absent you find him, in your absence, no sincere adviser.)
al-Zamakhsharī said: "He confined himself to one of them, namely the second, seeking generality and the inclusion of everything for which a son was claimed; or it is from دعا in the sense [of نسب, 'ascribe'] [Translator's note: the word نسب is missing in the source quotation], whose reflexive (muṭāwiʿ) is what occurs in his saying ﷺ: «من ادعى إلى غير مواليه» ('whoever ascribes himself to other than his patrons'), and in the poet's saying:
إنا بني نهشل لا ندعي لأب ... عنه ولا هو لا بالأبناء يشرينا
(We, the Banū Nahshal, do not ascribe ourselves to any father in place of him, nor would he sell us for other sons.)
i.e. we are not ascribed to him [Translator's note: so in the source; i.e. to another father]."
(وَما يَنْبَغِي لِلرَّحْمنِ أَنْ يَتَّخِذَ وَلَداً): the wāw is circumstantial or a conjunction; ما is negating; ينبغي is an imperfect verb and للرحمن is attached to it; أن يتخذ is an interpreted maṣdar in the position of the nominative as the agent; and ولدا is the direct object.
(إِنْ كُلُّ مَنْ فِي السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ إِلَّا آتِي الرَّحْمنِ عَبْداً): إن is negating; كل is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and من is the muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct); في السموات والأرض is attached to an omitted element that is the ṣila of من. It is also possible that من is an indefinite noun qualified by the preposition and its genitive noun, because it occurs after كل, an indefinite — and this is perhaps preferable. إلا is a particle of restriction; آتي الرحمن is the khabar; and عبدا is a ḥāl of the latent pronoun in آتي.
(لَقَدْ أَحْصاهُمْ وَعَدَّهُمْ عَدًّا): the lām prepares for the oath; قد is a particle of realization; أحصاهم is a verb, a latent agent and a direct object; عدهم is conjoined to أحصاهم; and عدا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq.
(وَكُلُّهُمْ آتِيهِ يَوْمَ الْقِيامَةِ فَرْداً): the wāw is a conjunction; كلهم is a mubtadaʾ and آتيه its khabar. When كل is annexed to an explicitly stated definite noun, as in كلهم and كل الناس, what has been transmitted is that the pronoun may refer back to it in the singular according to the wording of كل, so you say كلكم ذاهب, and it may refer back in the plural in consideration of the meaning, so you say كلكم ذاهبون. If, however, the definite noun annexed to it is omitted, both ways have been heard from the Arabs — because some denied the first. يوم القيامة is an adverb attached to آتيه, and فردا is a ḥāl.
(إِنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحاتِ سَيَجْعَلُ لَهُمُ الرَّحْمنُ وُدًّا): إن and its noun; the clause آمنوا is the ṣila and the clause عملوا الصالحات is conjoined to آمنوا; the clause سيجعل is the khabar of إن; لهم is the second object of يجعل; الرحمن is the agent; and ودا is the first object of يجعل. This "making" is, naturally, with respect to this world, i.e. He plants affection [for them] in [people's] hearts without their seeking to gain affection.
(فَإِنَّما يَسَّرْناهُ بِلِسانِكَ لِتُبَشِّرَ بِهِ الْمُتَّقِينَ وَتُنْذِرَ بِهِ قَوْماً لُدًّا): the fāʾ is the faṣīḥa (the fāʾ indicating an implied clause), because it is conjoined to something implied, as if it were said: convey this that has been sent down to you, give glad tidings with it and warn, for We have only made it easy. إنما is the restraining [mā] and the restrained [inna] (kāffa wa-makfūfa), and here it conveys the reason for this implied element. يسرناه is a past verb, its agent and its object; بلسانك is attached to an omitted ḥāl, i.e. "flowing [on your tongue]". لتبشر: the lām is for cause (taʿlīl); تبشر is an imperfect verb in the accusative by an implied أن after the lām of cause; به is attached to تبشر; المتقين is a direct object; تنذر is conjoined; به is attached to تنذر; قوما is a direct object; and لدا is an adjective.
(وَكَمْ أَهْلَكْنا قَبْلَهُمْ مِنْ قَرْنٍ): كم is the declarative (khabariyya) kam, a fronted object of أهلكنا; قبلهم is an adverb attached to أهلكنا; and من قرن is a tamyīz (specification), as already established. What is meant is a nation.
(هَلْ تُحِسُّ مِنْهُمْ مِنْ أَحَدٍ أَوْ تَسْمَعُ لَهُمْ رِكْزاً): هل is a particle of the interrogative of denial (istifhām inkārī); تحس is an imperfect verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "you"; منهم is a ḥāl, because it was [originally] an adjective of أحد; من is a redundant (zāʾida) preposition; أحد is genitive by من in form and a direct object, accusative in position. أو is a conjunction; تسمع is conjoined to تحس; لهم is a ḥāl; and ركزا is a direct object.

* Rhetoric:
The closing verses of Sūrat Maryam contain several devices:
The first: repetition (al-takrār). The name الرحمن is repeated, as we said, sixteen times in the surah, most of them in its closing verses. Its benefit is that He alone is the All-Merciful; no one else deserves this name, and He has created for them all the needs on which their livelihood depends. So has man taken heed? Or is the veil still drawn over his eyes and deafness covering his ears? Whoever ascribes a son to Him has made Him like created human beings, and thereby put Him outside of deserving this name, which befits Him alone.
The second: iltifāt (shift of address) in His saying «لقد جئتم»: it turns from the third person to the second person in order to confront them face to face with the abhorrent thing they committed and the astonishing innovation they perpetrated.

* Benefits:
1- We said that the views of the grammarians are confused on His saying «لا يملكون الشفاعة» to the end of the verse. We have chosen what we consider — in our view — the soundest of the aspects, and we now quote some glimpses of their views, with comments suited to the occasion. al-Zamakhsharī — and the infallible one is exalted [above error] — entangled himself with his saying, "It is possible that it — i.e. the wāw in يملكون — is a sign of the plural, like the one in أكلوني البراغيث ('the fleas ate me')", in two respects. The first is that he ascribed to the Qur'an, which is the most eloquent of speech, the worst and most objectionable of dialects, whose ugliness has become proverbial. The second is that if he makes it a sign [of plurality] for من, then he has disclosed its meaning and stated plainly that it covers a plural, and then he refers back to its wording in the singular with the pronoun of اتخذ. So there is reference to its wording after reference to its meaning in a way that contradicts it, which is objectionable to them, because it is summarizing after clarifying; that reverses the path of eloquence, whose clear road is clarifying after summarizing.
al-Bayḍāwī said: "«إلا من اتخذ عند الرحمن عهدا»: except one who is adorned with that by which he is made ready and becomes worthy to intercede for the disobedient, namely faith and righteous deeds, according to what Allah the Exalted has promised; or except one who has taken from Allah permission for it, as in the saying of the Exalted:
«لا تَنْفَعُ الشَّفاعَةُ إِلَّا مَنْ أَذِنَ لَهُ الرَّحْمنُ» — from their saying عهد الأمير إلى فلان بكذا, when he commanded him to do it. The position is nominative as a badal of the pronoun, or accusative on the estimation of a muḍāf, i.e. except the intercession of one who has taken." This is similar to the opinion we inclined to, except that he inclined to the view that the exception is disconnected [Translator's note: so in the source]. The words of Abū Ḥayyān are: "The pronoun in لا يملكون refers to creation, indicated by the mention of the God-fearing and the criminals, since they are its two divisions. The exception is connected, and من is a badal of that pronoun or accusative as excepted; and لا يملكون is a resumptive statement." Then he cited numerous views which we pass over.
Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "لا يملكون is a ḥāl; إلا من اتخذ is in the position of the accusative as a disconnected exception. It was also said that it is connected, the pronoun in يملكون being for the God-fearing and the criminals; and it was said that it is in the position of the nominative as a badal of the pronoun in يملكون."
In al-Karkhī, the commentator on al-Jalālayn: "His saying 'i.e. people': he estimated it so as to pave the way for making the exception in His saying «إلا من اتخذ» connected [Translator's note: the source has منصلا, a misprint for متصلا], because of what the mention of the two groups, the God-fearing and the criminals, indicates, since they are its two divisions. It was also said that the pronoun of يملكون refers to the criminals, meaning the unbelievers. Some said: they will not be able to intercede for others as the believers are able." What has preceded is sufficient for us, for the field of discussion has grown long.
2- Returning to the verse of al-Farazdaq:
We return to the verse of al-Farazdaq. It is from some lines of his in which he apologizes for what happened on his part during a journey with his guide ʿĀṣim al-ʿAnbarī when he lost the way. The lines are:
فلما تصافنا الأداوة أجهشت ... إلى غضون العنبري الجراضم
فجاء بجلمود له مثل رأسه ... ليشرب ماء القوم بين الصرائم
على حالة لو أن في القوم حاتما ... على جوده لضنّ بالماء حاتم
(When we shared out the water-skin by measure, the wrinkles of the gluttonous ʿAnbarī were on the verge of tears to me; then he brought a rock-hard vessel of his, like his head, to drink the people's water among the sand-dunes — in such a state that, were Ḥātim among the people, for all his generosity Ḥātim would have been stingy with the water.)
التصافن is sharing out a little water by means of the صفن, a small vessel for ablution and the like. الأداوة is a water container, plural أداوى. Making the sharing fall on it is figurative (majāz), because it is the place of the water, and what is meant is "we shared out the water"; so it is a majāz mursal (metonymic trope) whose relationship is that of place (maḥalliyya). الجهش and الإجهاش are a person's turning to another in supplication and readying himself to weep to him, like a child to its mother. غضون الجلد are the creases of the skin; ascribing الإجهاش to them is a majāz ʿaqlī (rational trope), or also a majāz mursal whose relationship is place, because they are where its effect appears. الجراضم is one with a wide belly who eats much. By الجلمود is meant a large hard vessel like his head, i.e. the head of al-ʿAnbarī — a brilliant allusion to his stupidity, because an excessively large head is a sign of dullness, and in the hardness there is also an allusion to that. His saying بين الصرائم: the plural of صريمة, which is the end of a stretch of sand — an indication that they were in a trackless desert with no water, in such a straitened state that, were it established in that state that Ḥātim was among the people, despite his famous generosity he would have been stingy with the water. على means في ("in"); and the transmission of al-Mubarrad in his al-Kāmil is على ساعة ("at a time").

dervis-irab:1-6.t:
* Vocabulary:
(وَهَنَ): in al-Miṣbāḥ: "wahana yahinu, of the pattern waʿada: he became weak, so he is wāhin in the matter, in work and in body. Wahantuhu means I weakened him — it is transitive, and in one dialect intransitive — so he is mawhūn of body and bone; but it is better to make it transitive with the hamza, saying:
awhantuhu. Al-wahan, with two fatḥas, is a dialectal form of the maṣdar, and wahina yahinu, with two kasras, is a dialectal form. Abū Zayd said: I heard among the Bedouin someone reading «فما وهنوا» [with kasra]." In al-Qāmūs and elsewhere: wahanahu yahinuhu wahnan and awhanahu mean he weakened him; wahana and awhana al-rajul means the man entered the wahn of the night; [then a series of dialectal forms:] wahana and wahuna yahinu, and wahina yawhanu wahnan and wahanan, and wahuna yawhunu wahnan: he became weak in a matter, in work or in body; tawahhana al-baʿīr: the camel lay down; [tawahhana] al-ṭāʾir: the bird became too heavy from eating carrion to be able to rise. Al-wahn is a maṣdar; and of men or camels it means the thick-set and short; al-wahn of the night is about its middle, or after an hour of it; al-mawhin of the night is like al-wahn; and al-wahnāna among women is one too lazy for work through a life of ease.
(الْمَوالِيَ): those next to me in lineage, such as paternal cousins. Al-mawālī is the plural of mawlā, who is the ʿāṣib (agnatic heir).
(عاقِراً): one who does not give birth. He said in al-Qāmūs: "ʿaqurat taʿqur ʿuqran and ʿaqran and ʿaqāran, and ʿaqirat taʿqar ʿaqaran and ʿaqāratan and ʿaqāra, and ʿuqirat al-marʾa or al-nāqa: the woman or she-camel became barren, i.e. her womb was held back and she did not give birth; ʿaqira ʿaqaran al-amr: the matter produced no outcome; and ʿaqira ʿaqaran al-rajul: the man was dumbfounded."
(وَلِيًّا): a son — this is one of its many meanings.

* I'rab:
(كهيعص،) (ذِكْرُ رَحْمَتِ رَبِّكَ عَبْدَهُ زَكَرِيَّا): (كهيعص) — the discussion of the openings of the surahs, their i'rab and their meanings has been given before, so refer back to it. (ذكر) is the khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject), i.e. "this which is recited to you of the Qur'an", or a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted, i.e. "in what is recited to you is a mention". (رحمة ربك) is put in construct with (ذكر), as a maṣdar (verbal noun) in construct with its object, the agent being latent (mustatir), i.e. "Allah's mention of the mercy of His servant Zechariah" [Translator's note: so in the source]. (عبده) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) of (رحمة), and (زكريا) is a badal (substitute) from (عبده) or ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition) to it.
(إِذْ نادى رَبَّهُ نِداءً خَفِيًّا): (إذ) is an adverb (ẓarf) for past time, attached (mutaʿalliq) to (رحمة ربك), i.e. Allah's mercy upon him at the time he called Him. It has also been said that what governs it is (ذكر), and it has also been said that it is a badal ishtimāl (substitute of inclusion) from (زكريا). The clause (نادى) is the one to which the adverb is put in construct; the fāʿil (agent) is latent, implied as "he"; (نداء) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object); and (خفيا) is an adjective.
(قالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي وَهَنَ الْعَظْمُ مِنِّي وَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْباً): (رب) is a vocative put in construct with the omitted yāʾ of the first person; (إنّ) and its noun, and the clause (وهن العظم) is its khabar; (مني) is a ḥāl (circumstantial); (اشتعل) is conjoined to (وهن); (الرأس) is the fāʿil; and (شيبا) is a tamyīz (specification) converted from the agent, i.e. grey hair spread in my head. The secret of this metaphor will come under Rhetoric.
(وَلَمْ أَكُنْ بِدُعائِكَ رَبِّ شَقِيًّا): the wāw is conjunctive; (لم) is a particle of negation, conversion and jussive; (أكن) is a defective imperfect verb, jussive (majzūm) by (لم), its noun latent, implied as "I"; (شقيا) is its khabar; (بدعائك) is attached to (شقيا); and (رب) is a vocative in construct with the omitted yāʾ of the first person.
(وَإِنِّي خِفْتُ الْمَوالِيَ مِنْ وَرائِي وَكانَتِ امْرَأَتِي عاقِراً): (وإني) is conjoined to (إني وهن); the yāʾ is the noun of (إنّ) and the clause (خفت) is its khabar; (الموالي) is the mafʿūl bihi; and (من ورائي) is attached to something omitted, or to the sense of guardianship (wilāya) in (الموالي). It may not be attached to (خفت), because the meaning would be corrupt. The reason for the corruption is that the fear is occurring in the present, not in the future; if (من ورائي) were made attached to (خفت), the fear would have to be occurring in the future, i.e. after his death — which, as you see, is plainly corrupt. Al-Zamakhsharī's words are: "(من ورائي): after my death. Ibn Kathīr read min warāya with the short vowel. This adverb is not attached to (خفت), because the meaning would be corrupt, but to something omitted, or to the sense of guardianship in (الموالي), i.e. I fear the doing of the kinsmen — namely their changing [things] and the evil of their succession — after me; or I fear those who will take charge of the affair after me. ʿUthmān, Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī and ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, may Allah be pleased with them, read khaffati al-mawālī min warāʾī ("the kinsmen have become few behind me"). This has two meanings. One is that warāʾī means behind me and after me, so the adverb is attached to (الموالي), i.e. they have become few and unable to uphold the affair of the religion, so he asked his Lord to strengthen and support them with an heir He would grant him. The second is that it means in front of me, so it is attached to khaffat, and he means that they have dwindled before him and passed away, and none of them remains through whom there could be strength and support." Ibn Hishām said in al-Mughnī: "The second is His saying, Exalted is He: «وإني خفت الموالي من ورائي», for what first comes to mind is that (من) is attached to (خفت), but that is corrupt in meaning. The correct view is that it is attached to (الموالي), because of the sense of guardianship it contains, i.e. 'I fear their guardianship after me and the evil of their succession'; or to something omitted that is a ḥāl from (الموالي), or [to something omitted] in construct with them, i.e. 'being after me', or 'the doing of the kinsmen after me'. As for whoever read khaffat, with fatḥa on the khāʾ, doubling of the fāʾ and kasra on the tāʾ, then (من) is attached to the verb mentioned." (وكانت امرأتي عاقرا): the wāw is conjunctive, and kāna with its noun and its khabar.
(فَهَبْ لِي مِنْ لَدُنْكَ وَلِيًّا): the fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa (implying an omitted condition), i.e. "and if not, then grant me"; (هب) is an imperative verb; (لي) is attached to (هب); (من لدنك) is a ḥāl; and (وليا) is the mafʿūl bihi of (هب).
(يَرِثُنِي وَيَرِثُ مِنْ آلِ يَعْقُوبَ وَاجْعَلْهُ رَبِّ رَضِيًّا): the clause (يرثني) is an adjective of (وليا), and that is why it is nominative; it has also been read in the jussive, as the response to the request. (يرث) is conjoined to (يرثني); (من آل يعقوب) is attached to (يرث); and the object of (يرث) is omitted, implied as "the law, wisdom and knowledge", because prophets do not bequeath wealth. It has also been said: "he will inherit from me the office of ḥabr (priesthood)" — he was a ḥabr — "and inherit from the family of Jacob the kingship"; on this view the yāʾ in (يرثني) is accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e. "inherits from me the priesthood". (اجعله) is a verb of supplication with a latent fāʿil; (رب) is a vocative in construct with the omitted yāʾ of the first person; and (رضيا) is the second mafʿūl bihi of (اجعل).
Some found the clause (يرثني) problematic as an adjective, on the basis that Allah's prophet John died before his father — [problematic] in that the prophet's supplication would then have gone unfulfilled, since by dying before him he did not inherit from him, and it is known what is inherited from prophets. This objector held that the clause is resumptive, not an adjective. The answer given is that the supplication of prophets may go unfulfilled: it happened to our Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ that he asked for three things; he was answered in two and the answer in the third was withheld. The resumptive view was objected to on the grounds that the clause would then convey a report, and the reports of the prophets never fail. The answer given is that this report was according to his strong supposition, because Allah's prophet Zechariah, being aged, strongly supposed that whenever he was granted a son, that son would inherit from him. Further, al-Jalāl al-Suyūṭī mentioned the problem in his book Sharḥ ʿUqūd al-Jumān, and mentioned an answer like the one we have just given; then he said: "Shaykh Bahāʾ al-Dīn answered that what is meant is inheriting prophethood and knowledge, and that happened in his [father's] lifetime." The Prophet ﷺ said: «إنا معاشر الأنبياء لا نورث» ("We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from"); al-Bazzāz [Translator's note: so in the source; usually al-Bazzār] narrated it with the wording "Naḥnu maʿāshir…", etc. The rest of the hadith is:
«ما تركناه صدقة» ("What we leave is charity"). (معاشر) is accusative by specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), governed by a verb that must be omitted, implied as "I specify"; in (ما تركناه), (ما) is a relative noun in the position of the nominative as the mubtadaʾ, (تركنا) is its ṣila (relative clause), the returning pronoun being omitted, i.e. "we left it", and (صدقة) is the khabar of (ما). The wisdom in prophets not being inherited from is that a person's heart may come to harbour a desire for the death of the one he will inherit from, in order to take his wealth; so Allah kept His prophets and their families above that; and so that no false person might think that they amass wealth for their heirs; and because they are like fathers to their community, so their wealth belongs to the whole community — which is the meaning of general charity. As for His saying, Exalted is He, «فَهَبْ لِي مِنْ لَدُنْكَ وَلِيًّا يَرِثُنِي وَيَرِثُ مِنْ آلِ يَعْقُوبَ», and His saying «وورث سليمان», what is meant is inheritance in knowledge and prophethood. By this the claim that non-inheritance is peculiar to our Prophet ﷺ is repelled. If it is said that Allah reported of one of them His saying:
«واني خفت الموالي», since one does not fear the kinsmen [taking] prophethood [Translator's note: the objection is elliptical in the source], the answer is that he feared from the kinsmen disagreement after him and turning away from the truth, so he wished for a son who would be a prophet to stand among them. There remains here something that must be pointed out, namely: do prophets inherit?
The author of al-Tatimma said: prophethood is a bar to inheritance. Al-Bazzāz the preacher mentioned that it was narrated: "We, the company of prophets, neither inherit nor are inherited from." This is contradicted by what al-Māwardī mentioned in al-Aḥkām al-Sulṭāniyya, that he ﷺ inherited from his father Umm Ayman the Abyssinian, whose name was Baraka, five camels, a flock of sheep, and his freedman Shuqrān, whose name was Ṣāliḥ and who was present at Badr; and he inherited from his mother her house, and from Khadīja her house.

* Rhetoric:
In these verses there are numerous devices, which we discuss briefly:

1- Iḥtirās (precautionary qualification) in His saying «نِداءً خَفِيًّا»
Discussion of it has been given before: it consists in the speaker's presenting a meaning against which an objection, ambiguity or misleading impression could be raised; he becomes aware of that while composing, and so brings into the body of the speech something that frees it from all that. Numerous examples of it have been given before, and similar counterparts will come. Here it is in the word (خفيا): he brought it out of regard for the way of Allah in keeping one's supplication hidden — since loud and hidden are the same to Allah, it was more fitting for him to guard against anything suggesting ostentation before people, who judge by appearances and are ignorant of the reality of inner thoughts; or so as not to be blamed for asking for a child at the time of old age and decrepitude, and to ward off the meddling that loosens tongues with all kinds of blame. It has also been said that he was guarding against his kinsmen whom he feared. And it has been said that there is no iḥtirās here at all, and that the speech runs on its literal sense, because the faintness of his voice resulted from his weakness and old age, when the voice grows faint, the tongue tires, the eyes grow dim and the ears grow heavy, as in the saying of ʿAwf ibn Muḥallim al-Khuzāʿī:
إن الثمانين وبلغتها ... قد أحوجت سمعي إلى ترجمان
(The eighty years — and may you reach them — have made my hearing need an interpreter.)
And it has been said in describing an old man: "His voice is a whisper, and his hearing comes and goes."

2- Al-istiʿāra al-makniyya (implicit metaphor):
In His saying, Exalted is He, «وَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْباً», He likened grey hair to flames of fire in its whiteness, its glare, its spreading through the hair, its pervading it and its taking hold of it in every way; then He cast it in the form of implicit metaphor, and attributed the blazing to the place of the hair and where it grows, which is the head. He brought out grey hair as the tamyīz, and did not put "head" in construct, i.e. did not say "my head", relying on the addressee's knowledge that it was Zechariah's head. Hence this sentence became eloquent and was attested as rhetorically excellent. We add to that the four points of resemblance latent in this far-reaching image, which are:
a- Speed: when fire blazes and its tongues leap out, it rapidly devours whatever it reaches; and likewise grey hair has hardly streaked the head before it spreads with astonishing speed.
b- Impossibility of remedy: when fire breaks out, its torrent surges and its flames fly, it sweeps away everything it meets, and rock and wood are humbled before it, as in the saying of Abū Tammām:
لقد تركت أمير المؤمنين بها ... للنار يوما ذليل الصخر والخشب
(You left there, O Commander of the Believers, a day for the fire on which rock and wood were humbled.)
Rock submits to it, wood is humbled, and everything it reaches surrenders to its torrent, with no stratagem availing against it; the fireman may find it impossible to quench its flames, and often water becomes like firewood that kindles it. Likewise grey hair spreads with strange speed through the parts of the head and persists in its speed, so that remedying it is difficult — indeed impossible. Often those afflicted with greyness resort to covering their grey with false dyes to hide the truth about themselves and to captivate the hearts of beautiful women, but that will change nothing of the actual reality.
c- Pain: just as fire is burning and searing and pains whoever touches it, so grey hair pains the grey-haired man, when beautiful women turn away from him and eyes look down on him, as in the saying of Ibn al-Rūmī:
وكنت جلاء للعيون من القذى ... فقد أصبحت تقذي بشيبي وترمد
هي الأعين النجل التي كنت تشتكي ... مواقعها في القلب والرأس أسود
(I used to clear eyes of their motes; now they are irritated and inflamed by my grey hair. They are the same wide eyes whose striking in the heart I used to complain of when my head was black.)
And the saying of Abū Tammām:
يا نسيب الثغام ذنبك أبقى ... حسناتي عند الحسان ذنوبا
لو رأى الله أن في الشيب خيرا ... جاورته الأبرار في الخلد شيبا
(O kinsman of the white thaghām plant [grey hair], your sin has left my good deeds as sins in the eyes of the fair. Had Allah seen any good in grey hair, the righteous would dwell near Him in eternity grey-haired.)
All of that is taken from ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa:
رأين الغواني الشيب لاح بعوارضي ... فأعرضن عني بالخدود النواضر
(The beautiful women saw grey hair gleam on my cheeks, and turned their fresh cheeks away from me.)
May Allah have mercy on Shawqī, when he sat on the banks of the Bardūnī in Zaḥla, listened to the whisperings of jewellery and the tinklings of bracelets, and found himself climbing towards seventy, and cried out:
شيعت أحلامي بقلب باك ... ولمت من طرق الملاح شباكي
ورجعت أدراج الشباب وورده ... أمشي مكانهما على الأشواك
وبجانبي واه كأن خفوقه ... لمّا تلفت جهشة المتباكي
(I saw off my dreams with a weeping heart, and gathered my nets from the paths of the fair; I turned back from the ways of youth and its roses, walking in their place upon thorns; and at my side is a frail [heart] whose throbbing, when I look back, is like the sob of one forcing tears.)
d- The end: just as the end of fire, after it has done its work and reached its limit, is extinction and going out — ashes — so too is the end of man; and that end is grievous enough to the soul and painful enough to the heart. These, then, are four qualities joining the thing likened and that to which it is likened. So reflect on this section, for it has excellence over all the other sections.
Further, we spoke briefly about the non-construct use of "head", relying on the addressee's knowledge; it must now be clarified. We say that metaphor has three aims:
exaggeration in the simile, clarity, and concision. Every metaphor achieves one of these aims; but this metaphor has achieved all three aims fully. For [the basic form of] the speech [Translator's note: the source reads «فإن الكلام أن يقال», evidently for «فإن أصل الكلام أن يقال»] would be to say: "The hair of the head became grey". Had the speech come thus, it would have conveyed clarity only, without exaggeration. The first wording conveys the greyness covering every part of the head — just as when you say "The fire of the house blazed", that is true of the fire blazing in some parts of it and not the rest, unlike when you say "The house blazed with fire", whose sense is that the fire encompassed the whole house in all its parts. So take note of this section, even if it has run somewhat long, for, like beauty, it does not weary.
Ibn Durayd borrowed "the head blazed with grey hair" and said in his Maqṣūra:
واشتعل المبيض في مسودّه ... مثل اشتعال النار في جزل الغضا
(The white blazed in its black like fire blazing in thick ghaḍā wood.)
Further, since greyness was for them a defect, they said "huwa ashyab", i.e. as an adjective contrary to the rule, because an adjective on the pattern afʿal comes only from faʿila, like fariḥa, and its condition is that it indicate defects or colours. Al-Shihāb al-Khafājī said that it is on the pattern of the adjective for physical afflictions, so they counted it among the defects. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Zawzanī has:
كفى الشيب عيبا ان صاحبه إذا ... أردت به وصفا له قلت أشيب
وكان قياس الأصل لو قلت شائبا ... ولكنه في جملة العيب يحسب
(It is enough of a defect in grey hair that, when you wish to describe its owner by it, you say "ashyab"; the regular form would be if you said "shāʾib", but it is reckoned among the defects.)
So shāʾib is an error and is not used.
Further, in His saying «واشتعل الرأس شيبا» there is the device of iṭnāb (amplification). First, He moved from "shikhtu" (I have grown old), which indicates weakness of body and greyness of head in summary, to this detail, for added confirmation. Second, from this rank to a third more eloquent than it, which is kināya (metonymy), which is more eloquent than plain statement. Third, from this rank to a fourth more eloquent in confirmation, which is building the kināya on a mubtadaʾ, i.e. your saying "I — the bones of my body have weakened". Fourth, from this rank to a fifth more eloquent, which is bringing (إنّ) onto the mubtadaʾ, I mean your saying "Indeed I — the bones of my body have weakened". Fifth, to a sixth rank, which is following the path of summary then detail, I mean "Indeed I — the bones have weakened, of my body". Sixth, to a seventh rank, which is dropping the mention of "body", to claim that the bones belong exclusively to the body so that there is no need to state "body" explicitly. Seventh, to an eighth rank, which is leaving the plural of "bone" for the singular, so that the weakness includes the bones one by one.

3- Tajrīd (abstraction):
That is in His saying, Exalted is He, «فَهَبْ لِي مِنْ لَدُنْكَ وَلِيًّا يَرِثُنِي وَيَرِثُ مِنْ آلِ يَعْقُوبَ».
We discussed it briefly before, and we shall now present it in full:
We say that tajrīd is that the speaker extracts from something possessing a quality another thing like it in that quality, by way of exaggeration of its perfection in it — as though it had reached such a degree in possessing that quality that another bearer of that quality could properly be extracted from it. It has divisions:
a- With the min of abstraction, as in their saying "I have in So-and-so (lī min fulān) a bosom friend". Among it is the noble verse. Similar is [a verse] of al-Qāḍī al-Fāḍil describing swords:
تمدا إلى الأعداء منها معاصسا ... فترجع من ماء الكلي بأساور
(They stretch wrists from them towards the enemies, and return with bracelets of the kidneys' blood.) [Translator's note: the first hemistich is garbled in the source; «معاصسا» is presumably «معاصما», "wrists".]
b- With the bāʾ of abstraction entering on what is extracted from, as in the saying of Ibn Hāniʾ:
وضربتم هام الكماة ورعتم ... بيض الخدور بكل ليث مخدر
(You struck the heads of armoured warriors and frightened the fair ones of the curtained chambers with every lion in its lair.)
And Abū Tammām said:
هتك الظلام أبو الوليد بغرة ... فتحت لنا باب الرجاء المقفل
بأتم من قمر السماء وإن بدا ... بدرا وأحسن في العيون وأجمل
وأجل من قس إذا استنطقته ... رأيا وألطف في الأمور وأجزل
(Abū al-Walīd tore the darkness with a radiant face that opened for us the locked door of hope — with one more complete than the moon of the sky, even when it appears full, finer and more beautiful in the eyes, and greater than Quss in judgement when you ask him to speak, subtler in affairs and more abundant.)
What is meant by "one more complete than the moon of the sky" is Abū al-Walīd himself.
c- With fī entering on what is extracted from, or on its pronoun, as in His saying, Exalted is He: «لَهُمْ فِيها دارُ الْخُلْدِ», i.e. in Hell, which is itself the abode of eternity; but He extracted from it another abode for exaggeration. And al-Mutanabbī said:
تمضي المواكب والأبصار شاخصة ... منها إلى الملك الميمون طائر
قد حرن في بشر في تاجه قمر ... في درعه أسد تدمى أظافره
(The processions pass with eyes from them fixed on the king of auspicious omen; they are bewildered by a man in whose crown is a moon, in whose coat of mail is a lion whose claws drip blood.)
The lion is the one praised himself, but he extracted from him another lion to magnify his affair and to exaggerate his possession of courage and assault.
d- With bayna, as in the saying of Ibn al-Nabīh:
يهتز بين وشاحيها قضيب نقا ... حمائم الحلي في أفنانه صدحت
(Between her two sashes sways a branch on a sand-hill, in whose boughs the doves of jewellery have warbled.)
e- And among them is that it be without the mediation of anything, as in the saying of Qatāda ibn Salama al-Ḥanafī:
فلئن بقيت لأرحلن بعزة ... تحوي الغنائم أو يموت كريم
(If I live on, I shall surely set out with a force that gathers spoils, or a noble man will die.)
By "a noble man" he meant himself, as though he extracted from himself a noble man by way of exaggerating his nobility; that is why he did not say "or I will die". And of Abū Tammām:
ولو تراهم وإيانا وموقفنا ... في موقف البين لاستهلالنا زجل
من حرقة أطلقتها فرقة أسرت ... قلبا ومن غزل في نحره عذل
وقد طوى الشوق في أحشائنا بقرا ... عينا طوتهن في أحشائها الكلل
(If you could see them and us and our standing at the place of parting, our weeping raised a clamour — from a burning that a parting released, which captured a heart, and from love-talk in whose throat was reproach; and longing had folded within our entrails wide-eyed wild cows [maidens], whom the curtains had folded within their own folds.)
What he means by the wide-eyed wild cows is those he first reported of in his saying "If you could see them", as though he extracted from them bearers of this quality, by way of exaggeration in it.
[Translator's note: the source lists the next item as «ز» (the seventh letter), skipping «و».]
g- And among them is that a person extracts from himself another person like him in the quality for which the speech is presented, and then addresses him, as in the saying of Abū al-Ṭayyib:
لا خيل عندك تهديها ولا مال ... فليسعد النطق إن لم يسعد الحال
(You have no horses to give, nor wealth; so let speech be generous if circumstances are not.)
It is as though he extracted from himself another person like him in lacking horses and wealth. Among it is the saying of al-Aʿshā:
ودّع هريرة إن الركب مرتحل ... وهل تطيق وداعا أيها الرجل
(Bid farewell to Hurayra, for the caravan is departing — but can you bear a farewell, O man?)
And Abū Nuwās said, excelling in love poetry:
يا كثير النوح في الدمن ... لا عليها بل على السكن
سنة العشّاق واحدة ... فإذا أحببت فاستنن
(O you who lament much at the ruined camps — not for them, but for the one who dwelt there: the way of lovers is one, so when you love, follow it.)
He means to address himself, and that is why he said after it:
ظن بي من قد كلفت به ... فهو يجفوني على الظنن
بات لا يعنيه ما لقيت ... عين ممنوع من الوسن
رشأ لولا ملاحته ... خلت الدنيا من الفتن
(The one I am infatuated with suspected me, and so shuns me on suspicion; he spent the night unconcerned with what an eye denied sleep endured — a fawn but for whose charm the world would be free of trials.)
Tajrīd is frequent in poetry, and examples of it will come in other places in this book.

dervis-irab:7-15.t:
* Vocabulary:
(سَمِيًّا): al-samiyy is the one named; it is faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl. Its origin is samiyw: the yāʾ and the wāw came together, the first of them having sukūn, so the wāw was changed to yāʾ and the yāʾ was assimilated into it — i.e. one named Yaḥyā. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "This is evidence that beautiful (sunuʿ) names deserve preference; it was these the Arabs aimed at in naming, because they are more distinguished, more eminent, and further from [giving rise to] nicknames — so that someone said in praise of a people:
سنع الأسامي مسبلي أزر ... حمر تمس الأرض بالهدب
(Of beautiful names, letting down red waist-wrappers that touch the ground with their fringes.)"
End of al-Zamakhsharī's words. Sunuʿ al-asāmī means their names are beautiful. One says sanuʿa al-rajul, like ẓarufa, so he is sanīʿ, i.e. handsome, and asnaʿ; the woman is sanʿāʾ; and sunʿ is the plural of asnaʿ, like ḥumr as the plural of aḥmar — from al-sanāʿa, which is beauty, as al-Ṣiḥāḥ states; i.e. their names are beautiful, so they are more distinguished, more eminent and further from nicknames. Ḥumr is an adjective of the waist-wrappers, and tamassu is another adjective of them. The hudb of a thing is its edge; what suits the meaning is that the plural is intended. Its ḍamma-form may be singular, like qufl, and plural, like fulk; and it may be a collective noun, which is why its singular came as hudba. Touching the ground with the edges is a kināya (metonymy) for their length — indeed for their wealth. It has also been said that al-samiyy means the like, the similar, the counterpart and the equal, as in al-Qāmūs and elsewhere, so each of the two is the samiyy of the other. Similar to Yaḥyā ("he lives") among their names are Yaʿmur and Yaʿīsh, if the naming is Arabic; they also named people Yamūt ("he dies") — he is Yamūt ibn al-Muzarraʿ. It has also been said that it is a diptote for being a proper name and foreign.
(عِتِيًّا): in al-Mukhtār: "ʿatā, of the pattern samā, [maṣdar ʿutuww] and also ʿutiyy and ʿitiyy, with ḍamma or kasra on the ʿayn; he is ʿātin, and al-ʿātī is one who exceeds the bounds in arrogance. ʿAtā al-shaykh yaʿtū ʿutuwwan and ʿitiyyan, with ḍamma or kasra on the ʿayn: the old man grew old and declined." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "i.e. I have reached ʿitiyy, which is dryness and stiffness in the joints and bones, like a withered stick; one says ʿatā al-ʿūd and ʿasā (the stick dried up), because of old age and advanced years; or: I have reached of the stages and ranks of old age what is called ʿitiyy."
(آيَةً): a sign of my wife's pregnancy.
(الْمِحْرابِ): in al-Qāmūs: "al-miḥrāb: the upper room; the front of the house and its most honoured place; the imam's station in the mosque; and the place a king withdraws to, keeping apart from people." As for the miḥrāb known today — a hollow niche in the mosque wall in which the imam prays — it is a later innovation unknown to the Arabs, and calling it a miḥrāb is a convention of the jurists. This is what al-Shihāb said in his gloss on al-Bayḍāwī; but the lexical «المغني» [Translator's note: so in the source, evidently for «المعنى», "meaning"] that al-Fīrūzābādī mentioned applies to it, namely "the imam's station in the mosque".
(الْحُكْمَ): wisdom. From it is the saying of al-Nābigha:
واحكم كحكم فتاة الحي إذ نظرت ... إلى حمام شراع وارد الثمد
قالت: ألا ليتما هذا الحمام لنا ... إلى حمامتنا أو نصفه فقد
فحسّبوه فألفوه كما ذكرت ... ستا وستين لم تنقص ولم تزد
(Judge wisely, like the judgement of the girl of the tribe when she looked at doves flocking down to the shallow pool. She said: "Would that these doves were ours, added to our dove, and half of them — that would be enough." So they counted them and found them as she had said: sixty-six, neither fewer nor more.)
The girl who judged is Zarqāʾ al-Yamāma, proverbial for keenness of sight. She looked at doves hurrying to the water and said:
ليت الحمام ليه ... إلى حمامتيه
ونصفه قديه ... تم الحمام ميه
(Would that the doves were mine, added to my dove, and half of them — enough for me; the doves would make a hundred.)
They fell into a hunter's net, and they counted them and found them sixty-six doves; half of them is thirty-three; and when all were added to her dove, they made a hundred. Shirāʿ, with kasra on the shīn, is what is raised; from it the sail (al-shirāʿ) was named — something like a wide sheet that is raised and set up on a ship, so the winds blow into it and carry the ship along. It is also narrated sirāʿ, plural of sarīʿ (swift); he described it [the noun ḥamām] by it because it is plural in meaning, just as he described it with wārid, which is singular, because it is singular in form. (الحمام) and (أو نصفه) are narrated in the nominative, on (ليتما) being rendered inoperative, and in the accusative, on its being operative — because the redundant (ما) restrains inna and its sisters except layta, which may be made operative or inoperative. (أو) is in the sense of the wāw. (قد) is in the sense of ḥasb ("enough"), so it is a noun put in construct with the yāʾ of the first person without the nūn of protection, as one says ḥasbī. The fāʾ [in فقد] is redundant to improve the wording, like the fāʾ of faqaṭ, both meaning "stop there". (حسّبوه) is with doubling of the sīn, so that the verse is free of khabn, a kind of metrical variation that is faulty. It has also been said that al-ḥukm is reason; and it has been said prophethood, because Allah perfected his reason in his childhood and gave him revelation.
(وَحَناناً): i.e. mercy towards his parents and others, tenderness and compassion. The following was recited:
وقالت حنان ما أتى بك هاهنا ... أذو نسب أم أنت بالحي عارف
(She said: "Compassion! What brought you here? Are you a kinsman, or are you acquainted with the tribe?")
This verse is by Mundhir al-Kalbī, and before it — so that its meaning is coherent — is:
وأحدث عهد من أمينة نظرة ... على جانب العلياء إذ أنا واقف
(My latest meeting with Umayna was a glance at the side of al-ʿAlyāʾ while I stood there.)
He says: my most recent encounter — i.e. meeting and sight — with Umayna, my beloved (the diminutive of Āmina), was a glance of mine at her beside that spot while I was standing there, i.e. at the time of my standing there. This suggests that he was standing waiting to see her. When she saw him she said to him: ḥanān, i.e. "my attitude is compassion and mercy for you". This is one of the places where the mubtadaʾ (subject) must be omitted, because it is a maṣdar (verbal noun) transferred from the accusative. Her saying "What brought you here?"
is a question of wonder. "Are you a kinsman" means "Are you a man of kinship, or are you acquainted with this tribe?" (أذو نسب) may also be a badal (substitute) from the interrogative (ما), i.e. "What made you come here — or what guided you to it: a relative from the tribe, i.e. your acquaintance with it?" It is also possible that the question is genuine, which she related as if on someone else's tongue in order to prompt him with the answer by saying "Are you a kinsman", though she knew the reason for his coming, which was love for her — for perhaps one of her family might ask him, and he could answer with one of these two answers. It has also been said: compassion from Allah upon him. Ḥanna means he felt joy and longing, then it came to be used for kindness and tenderness. It has been said that Allah has ḥanān, just as it is said that He is raḥīm, by way of metaphor.
(عَصِيًّا): an intensive form. The origin of (عصيا) is ʿaṣīy[y] on the pattern faʿīl, the yāʾ being assimilated in it. The intensive form was brought to observe the verse-endings, because what is negated is the basis of disobedience, not intensity in it.

* I'rab:
(يا زَكَرِيَّا إِنَّا نُبَشِّرُكَ بِغُلامٍ اسْمُهُ يَحْيى): (يا) is the vocative particle, and (زكريا) is a single proper-name vocative, indeclinable (mabnī) on ḍamma; it has also been read Zakariyyāʾ with the hamza, according to the original form. (إنا) is inna and its noun; the clause (نبشرك) is its khabar (predicate), the kāf being the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (بغلام) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached (mutaʿalliq) to (نبشرك); (اسمه) is the mubtadaʾ and (يحيى) its khabar; and the nominal clause is an adjective of (غلام).
(لَمْ نَجْعَلْ لَهُ مِنْ قَبْلُ سَمِيًّا): the clause is a second adjective of (غلام); (له) is the second object of (نجعل); (من قبل) is a ḥāl (circumstantial); and (سميا) is the first object of (نجعل).
(قالَ رَبِّ أَنَّى يَكُونُ لِي غُلامٌ وَكانَتِ امْرَأَتِي عاقِراً وَقَدْ بَلَغْتُ مِنَ الْكِبَرِ عِتِيًّا): (رب) is a vocative in construct with the omitted yāʾ of the first person; (أنى) is an interrogative noun in the position of the accusative as an adverb of place, attached to the [notion of] settledness in the khabar of (يكون); (لي) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to the omitted fronted khabar of (يكون); and (غلام) is its postponed noun. (وكانت): the wāw is circumstantial; (كانت امرأتي عاقرا) is kāna with its noun and its khabar, and the clause is circumstantial. (وقد بلغت من الكبر) is also a circumstantial clause; (من الكبر) is attached to (بلغت), or to an omitted ḥāl from (عتيا), because it was an adjective of it and was fronted before it; and (عتيا) is the object of (بلغت). Pay no attention to the forced parsings the parsers have laboured over, such as parsing it as a ḥāl or a tamyīz (specification) with (من) redundant; this does not befit the Book of Allah.
(قالَ: كَذلِكَ قالَ رَبُّكَ هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ وَقَدْ خَلَقْتُكَ مِنْ قَبْلُ وَلَمْ تَكُ شَيْئاً): (قال) is a past verb whose fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir); it is said to refer to Allah the Exalted, and it is said to Gabriel. (كذلك) is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "the matter is thus"; or it is accusative by (قال), or by an omitted verb implied as "I will do thus"; the reference is to something vague explained by (هو عليّ هين). (قال ربك) is a verb and its fāʿil; (هو) is the mubtadaʾ; (علي) is attached to (هين); and (هين) is the khabar of (هو). «ولقد» [Translator's note: so in the source; the Qur'anic text is (وقد)]: the wāw is circumstantial and (قد) is a particle of affirmation; (خلقتك) is a verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; (من قبل) is attached to (خلقتك); the wāw is circumstantial; (لم) is a particle of negation, conversion and jussive; (تك) is a defective imperfect verb, jussive (majzūm) by (لم), the sign of its jussive being the implied sukūn on the nūn that was dropped for lightness; the noun of (تك) is latent; and (شيئا) is the khabar of (تك). The clause (ولم تك شيئا) is an overlapping ḥāl (ḥāl mutadākhila). The discussion of "thing" (shayʾ) between Ahl al-Sunna and the Muʿtazila, and al-Mutanabbī's skill in this area, will come.
(قالَ رَبِّ اجْعَلْ لِي آيَةً): (رب) is a vocative, whose i'rab has been given; (اجعل) is an imperative verb; (لي) is the second mafʿūl bihi; and (آية) is the first mafʿūl bihi.
(قالَ آيَتُكَ أَلَّا تُكَلِّمَ النَّاسَ ثَلاثَ لَيالٍ سَوِيًّا): (آيتك) is the mubtadaʾ; (أن) with what falls within its scope is the khabar; (الناس) is the mafʿūl bihi; (ثلاث ليال) is accusative as an adverb, the adverb being attached to (تكلم); and (سويا) is a ḥāl from the agent of (تكلم), i.e. "while you are without illness and sound of limb". It has also been said that (سويا) is accusative as an adjective of (ثلاث), meaning that they are complete.
(فَخَرَجَ عَلى قَوْمِهِ مِنَ الْمِحْرابِ فَأَوْحى إِلَيْهِمْ أَنْ سَبِّحُوا بُكْرَةً وَعَشِيًّا): the fāʾ is resumptive; (خرج) is a verb with a latent fāʿil; (على قومه) is attached to an omitted ḥāl; (من المحراب) is attached to (خرج); (فأوحى) is conjoined to (خرج); (أن) is explicative (tafsīriyya), because it comes after a clause containing the sense of saying; «وسبحوه» [Translator's note: so in the source; the Qur'anic text is (سبحوا), without a pronoun] is an imperative verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; (بكرة) is an adverb of time attached to (سبحوه); and (عشيا) is conjoined to (بكرة). (أن) may also be maṣdariyya (forming a maṣdar), the object of the revealing.
(يا يَحْيى خُذِ الْكِتابَ بِقُوَّةٍ وَآتَيْناهُ الْحُكْمَ صَبِيًّا): (يا يحيى) is a single proper-name vocative; (خذ الكتاب) is an imperative verb, a latent fāʿil and a mafʿūl bihi; (بقوة) is a ḥāl from the agent of (خذ), the bāʾ being for accompaniment (mulābasa), i.e. while you are clothed with strength and diligence. (وآتيناه): the wāw is resumptive, and (آتيناه) is a verb, its fāʿil and its first mafʿūl bihi; (الحكم) is the second mafʿūl bihi; and (صبيا) is a ḥāl from the hāʾ.
(وَحَناناً مِنْ لَدُنَّا وَزَكاةً وَكانَ تَقِيًّا): (وحنانا) is conjoined to (الحكم), i.e. "and We gave him ḥanān", i.e. mercy and tenderness in his heart and kindness towards others. It has also been said that it is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) of an omitted verb, but that is far-fetched. (من لدنا) is attached to an omitted adjective of (حنان); (زكاة) is conjoined to (حنانا); and (وكان تقيا) is conjoined to (آتيناه): kāna with its latent noun, and (تقيا) its khabar.
