(وَبَرًّا بِوالِدَيْهِ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ جَبَّاراً عَصِيًّا): (وبرا) is conjoined to (تقيا); (بوالديه) is attached to (برا); (ولم يكن) is conjoined to (وكان تقيا); the noun of (يكن) is latent, implied as "he"; (جبارا) is its khabar; and (عصيا) is a naʿt (adjective).
(وَسَلامٌ عَلَيْهِ يَوْمَ وُلِدَ وَيَوْمَ يَمُوتُ وَيَوْمَ يُبْعَثُ حَيًّا): the wāw is resumptive; (سلام) is the mubtadaʾ — beginning with it was permissible although it is indefinite because it contains the sense of supplication; (عليه) is the khabar; (يوم) is an adverb attached to (سلام); the clause (ولد) is put in construct with the adverb; what follows is conjoined to it; and (حيا) is a ḥāl.

* Rhetoric:
Ījāz (concision) in His saying, Exalted is He, «أَنَّى يَكُونُ لِي غُلامٌ». The outward form of the speech suggests that he considered unlikely what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had promised would happen; and it is not permissible for anyone — let alone a prophet — to utter what is not allowable or what outwardly gives a misleading impression. So the speech came concise, its implied sense being: "Will our strength and youth be restored to us so that we are granted a boy?" or "Will the child be from someone other than the barren wife?" Thus what was considered unlikely was the coming of a child from the two of them in their present state; but the answer removed the difficulty, for he was told: you two will have the child while you remain as you are.

* Benefits:
Ahl al-Sunna and the Muʿtazila disagreed about "thing" (shayʾ). The Muʿtazila believe that "thing" covers the existent and the non-existent whose existence is possible — so it does not cover the impossible. As for Ahl al-Sunna, for them "thing" covers only the existent. The verse testifies for Ahl al-Sunna, because His saying «وَلَمْ تَكُ شَيْئاً» is explicit in that. Al-Mutanabbī glanced at this disagreement from a hidden, distant angle and used it in describing a coward. That is in a highly regarded ode of his praising Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd al-Kilābī al-Manbijī, among what he composed in his youth. He said:
وضاقت الأرض حتى كادها ربهم ... إذا رأى غير شيء ظنه رجلا
(The earth grew so narrow that their fugitive [Translator's note: the source has «كادها ربهم»; the familiar text of the verse is «كان هاربهم»], whenever he saw a non-thing, thought it a man.)
His commentators overlooked the reality of the dispute raging between Ahl al-Sunna and the Muʿtazila, and went every which way in explaining this verse. Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ said:
"He was criticised for this verse, and it was said: How can he see a non-thing, when a non-thing is non-existent and the non-existent is not seen? There is a contradiction in it. But the matter is not as they said; rather he meant a thing of no account." Abū Bakr al-Khwārizmī said: "Seeing in this verse is not seeing with the eye; it is only seeing with the heart, by which he means imagining, and a non-thing may be imagined; there is much like it." Al-Wāḥidī said: "Whenever he saw something of no account, or not worth a thought, he took it for a man pursuing him — and such is the habit of the fearful fugitive, as in the saying of Jarīr:
ما زال يحسب كل شيء بعدهم ... خيلا تكر عليهم ورجالا
(After them he kept thinking every thing was horsemen charging upon them, and men.)
Abū ʿUbayd said: When Jarīr's verse was recited to al-Akhṭal, he said: By Allah, he stole it from their Book: «يحسبون كل صيحة عليهم» ("They think every shout is against them"). It is permissible to omit an adjective and leave the noun qualified to indicate it, as in his saying, upon him be blessing and peace: «لا صلاة لجار المسجد إلا في المسجد» ("There is no prayer for the neighbour of the mosque except in the mosque") — they agree that the meaning is: no complete, meritorious prayer. And they say "This is not a thing", meaning not a good thing. Some theologians said:
'Allah created things from no-thing (min lā shayʾ).' It was said: this is an error, because nothing is created from no-thing, and whoever says Allah creates from no-thing makes no-thing something from which [things] are created. The correct thing is to say: He creates not from a thing (lā min shayʾ), because when he says 'not from a thing' he denies that before His creating there was a thing from which He creates things." And the correct view is what he said: i.e. whenever he saw a non-thing to be feared. From this valley is «حتى إذا جاءه أم يجده شيئا» [Translator's note: so in the source; the Qur'anic text (al-Nūr 39) is «لم يجده شيئا»]: its meaning is [he did not find] what he wanted or sought, or what would suffice him in place of water, i.e. a thing that is useful and sufficient.

dervis-irab:66-72.t:
* Vocabulary:
(جِثِيًّا): with ḍamma or kasra on the jīm, and it was read with both; plural of jāthin, from jathā yajthū, ajthā and yajthī (two dialectal forms): that is, he sat on his knees or stood on the tips of his fingers; he is then jāthin.
(صِلِيًّا): with kasra or ḍamma on the ṣād, and it was read with both; a maṣdar (verbal noun) of ṣaliya (with kasra or fatḥa on the lām) al-nāra, that is, he entered the fire.

* I'rab:
(وَيَقُولُ الْإِنْسانُ أَإِذا ما مِتُّ لَسَوْفَ أُخْرَجُ حَيًّا): the wāw is resumptive; yaqūlu al-insānu is an imperfect verb and agent, and the al in it is generic; the hamza is for a question carrying the sense of negation; idhā is an adverb for the future time, attached to an omitted verb indicated by his words «لسوف أخرج», because the lām prevents it from being attached to the overt «أخرج», since what follows it does not govern what precedes it; mā is redundant; the clause «مت» is a ṣila (relative clause); the lām is the lām of inceptive emphasis (lām al-ibtidāʾ); sawfa is a particle of futurity; ukhraju is a passive imperfect verb and its nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "anā"; ḥayyan is a ḥāl (circumstantial). It is permissible for the lām, which makes the verb purely present, and sawfa, which makes it purely future, to occur together because the lām here is merely for emphasis. The lām was stripped of its meaning to suit sawfa, and sawfa was not stripped of its meaning to suit the lām, because if this were reversed sawfa would become void, since it has no meaning other than futurity; as for the lām, when it is stripped of the present sense, emphasis remains for it, so it is not voided. (أَوَلا يَذْكُرُ الْإِنْسانُ أَنَّا خَلَقْناهُ مِنْ قَبْلُ وَلَمْ يَكُ شَيْئاً): «أولا»: the hamza is for a question of denial, the wāw is a conjunction, and lā is negative; yadhkuru is an imperfect verb conjoined to «يقول»; the hamza of denial was placed between the conjoined-to element and the conjunction; al-insānu is the agent; annā: anna and its noun, and the clause «خلقناه» is the khabar of anna; anna and what follows it are in the position of an interpreted maṣdar, the object of yadhkuru; min qablu, the preposition and its genitive noun, are attached to yadhkuru; wa-lam: the wāw is a ḥāl wāw, and lam is a particle of negation, reversal and jussive; yaku is an imperfect verb jussive by lam, the sign of its jussive being the implied sukūn on the nūn omitted for lightening; its noun is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "huwa"; shayʾan is the khabar of yaku. The muḍāf ilayhi of qablu is omitted, its implied form being "before the state he is in", that is, the state of his existence; some of them implied "before his resurrection". (فَوَ رَبِّكَ لَنَحْشُرَنَّهُمْ وَالشَّياطِينَ): the fāʾ is a conjunction and the wāw is for an oath; rabbika is genitive by the wāw of the oath, and the two are attached to an omitted verb, its implied form being "uqsimu" (I swear); the benefit of this oath will come in the chapter on Rhetoric; the lām occurs in the response to the oath; la-naḥshurannahum is an imperfect verb indeclinable on fatḥa because of its attachment to the heavy nūn of emphasis, and the agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "naḥnu"; the hāʾ is the direct object; al-shayāṭīna is conjoined to the hāʾ, or the wāw means "with" and al-shayāṭīna is a mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment). (ثُمَّ لَنُحْضِرَنَّهُمْ حَوْلَ جَهَنَّمَ جِثِيًّا): thumma is a conjunction of delay; la-nuḥḍirannahum is conjoined to «لنحشرنهم»; ḥawla is an adverb of place attached to «نحضرنهم»; jahannama is a muḍāf ilayhi; jithiyyan is a ḥāl. (ثُمَّ لَنَنْزِعَنَّ مِنْ كُلِّ شِيعَةٍ أَيُّهُمْ أَشَدُّ عَلَى الرَّحْمنِ عِتِيًّا): thumma la-nanziʿanna is conjoined to «لنحضرنهم»; min kulli shīʿatin, the two are attached to «ننزعن»; ayyuhum is a relative noun meaning "alladhī", and its vowel according to Sībawayh is a vowel of indeclinability because it departed from its peers, that is, because it was annexed and the head of its ṣila was omitted; it is in the position of accusative as the direct object of «لننزعن»; ashaddu is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, and the clause is the ṣila, the implied form being "huwa ashaddu"; ʿitiyyan is a tamyīz (specification); ʿalā al-Raḥmāni, the two are attached to «أشد» or to an omitted ḥāl. Further discussion of this verse will come in the chapter on Benefits. (ثُمَّ لَنَحْنُ أَعْلَمُ بِالَّذِينَ هُمْ أَوْلى بِها صِلِيًّا): thumma is a conjunction of order and delay; the lām is for inception; naḥnu is the mubtadaʾ and aʿlamu the khabar; bi-alladhīna, the two are attached to aʿlamu; hum is a mubtadaʾ and awlā the khabar, and the clause is the ṣila; bihā, the two are attached to awlā; and ṣiliyyan is a tamyīz. It was also said that ṣiliyyan is the plural of ṣālin, and so is accusative as a ḥāl. In the tamyīz there is a benefit, namely specification by severity of punishment, not specification by the very fact of punishment, since they all share in it. (وَإِنْ مِنْكُمْ إِلَّا وارِدُها كانَ عَلى رَبِّكَ حَتْماً مَقْضِيًّا): the wāw is a conjunction and in is negative; minkum is an adjective of an omitted mubtadaʾ, its implied form being "aḥad", that is, "there is none of you"; illā is a particle of restriction; wāriduhā is the khabar; kāna is a defective past verb and its noun is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "huwa", that is, the arrival; ḥatman is its khabar and maqḍiyyan is an adjective of ḥatman. (ثُمَّ نُنَجِّي الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا وَنَذَرُ الظَّالِمِينَ فِيها جِثِيًّا): thumma nunajjī is conjoined to what preceded, and the agent of nunajjī is latent, its implied form being "naḥnu"; alladhīna is a relative noun, the object, and ittaqaw is the ṣila; wa-nadharu is conjoined to nunajjī and the agent is latent, its implied form being "naḥnu"; al-ẓālimīna is the direct object; fīhā, the two are attached to nadharu or to jithiyyan, and it may be attached to an omitted element as a ḥāl from jithiyyan, because it is originally an adjective of an indefinite noun that was put before it and so became accusative as a ḥāl; and jithiyyan is a ḥāl, or you may make it a second object of nadharu, that is, "we leave them in it kneeling".

* Rhetoric:
1- The art of the oath:
In His saying, Exalted is He, «فَوَ رَبِّكَ لَنَحْشُرَنَّهُمْ» there is the art of the oath, which is that the speaker wishes to swear about something and so swears by what brings him pride and glorification of his standing, or exaltation of his worth, or by what constitutes a censure of another, or runs in the manner of amatory verse and tenderness, or comes out in the manner of admonition and asceticism. The oath here conveys two things: first, that custom has it that a report is confirmed by an oath; and second, that in Allah the Exalted swearing by His own name annexed to His Messenger ﷺ there is an elevation of the latter's rank and exaltation of his standing, just as the standing of the heaven and the earth was raised in His saying «فَوَ رَبِّ السَّماءِ وَالْأَرْضِ إِنَّهُ لَحَقٌّ». The verification of that will come in its places.
The poets expanded on the oath, because it has sweetness and raises the standing of the one celebrated in amatory verse. How graceful is the saying of ʿAbd al-Muḥsin al-Ṣūrī, one of the most masterly I have heard (the source reads «سمغنا»):
يا غزالا قد رمى باللحظ ... قلبي فأصابا
(O gazelle who shot my heart with a glance and hit the mark)
بالذي ألهم تعذيبي ... ثناياك العذابا
(By Him who inspired my torment, [and made] your teeth sweet and cool)
والذي ألبس خديك ... من الورد نقابا
(And by Him who clothed your cheeks in a veil of roses)
والذي أودع في فيك من الشهد شرابا
(And by Him who placed in your mouth a drink of honey)
والذي صيّر حظي ... منك هجرا واجتنابا ما الذي قالته عينا ... ك لقلبي فأجابا
(And by Him who made my share of you abandonment and avoidance: what did your eyes say to my heart, and it answered?)
And Ibn Khafāja al-Andalusī said:
لا وسحر بين أجفانكم ... فتن الحب به من فتنا
(No, by the magic between your eyelids, by which love has tempted those it tempted)
وحديث من مواعيدكم ... تحسد العين عليه الأذنا
(And by a talk of your promises, for which the eye envies the ear)
ما رحلت العيس عن أرضكم ... فرأت عيناي شيئا حسنا
(The camels did not depart from your land, but that my eyes saw something beautiful)
And al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Aḥnaf reached the utmost with his saying:
واني ليرضيني قليل نوالكم ... وإن كان لا أرضى لكم بقليل
(I am content with your little favour, though I would not be content with little for you)
بحرمة ما قد كان بيني وبينكم ... من الود إلا عدتم بجميل
(By the sanctity of the affection that was between me and you, return [to me] with kindness)
And Abū al-Ṭayyib was inventive with his saying:
أحيا وأيسر ما قاسيت ما قتلا ... والبين جار على ضعفي وما عدلا
(I live, though the least of what I suffered would kill; and separation wronged my weakness and was not just)
والوجد يقوى كما تقوى النوى أبدا ... والصبر ينحل في جسمي كما نحلا
(And longing grows strong as the parting grows strong forever, and patience wastes away in my body as I have wasted away)
لولا مفارقة الأحباب ما وجدت ... لها المنايا إلى أرواحنا سبلا
(Were it not for parting from loved ones, death would have found no ways to our souls)
بما بجفنيك من سحر صلي دنفا ... يهوى الحياة وأما إن صددت فلا
(By the magic in your eyelids, be kind to one who is sick, who loves life; but if you turn away, then not)

2- Iftinān (the combining of different kinds):
That is in His saying, Exalted is He, «ثُمَّ نُنَجِّي الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا وَنَذَرُ الظَّالِمِينَ فِيها جِثِيًّا». Iftinān is that the speaker diversifies and brings in his speech two kinds, either opposites, or different, or alike; and the verse before us combines two opposites: it combines promise and threat, glad tidings and warning, together with what these two kinds entail of praise for those singled out for the glad tidings and censure for the people of the warning. Many examples of it will come in the Noble Qur'an.
Among the combinations of opposites in poetry is the saying of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāhir ibn al-Ḥusayn, which al-Kāmil attributes to Abū Dulaf:
أحبك يا ظلوم وأنت مني ... مكان الروح من جسد الجبان
(I love you, O Ẓalūm, and you are to me as the soul is to the body of a coward)
ولو أني أقول مكان روحي ... خشيت عليك بادرة الطعان
(And were I to say "as my soul", I would fear for you the sudden thrust of the spear)
See how he combined in this poetry amatory verse and martial boasting; the amatory is gentleness and the martial is severity. And ʿAntara said, and excelled:
إن تغد في دوني القناع فانني ... طب بأخذ الفارس المستلئم
(If you let down the veil before me, I am skilled in seizing the armoured horseman)
This is among the best that has been said in this field, for in it he combined amatory verse and martial boasting, earnestness and jest, and brought in a delightful anecdote and a rare novelty, when, after describing her screening her face from him with the veil until what lay between his sight and her face was like the draping night that stands between eyes and things seen, he said: "I am skilled in seizing the armoured horseman". He says: if you veil yourself from me, I, by my experience of war, am expert in seizing the horseman whose armour has screened him and come between me and fighting him. So he put earnestness forth in the form of jest, and his verse came with iftinān as well as a delightful witticism, and he expressed his subtle meaning in this noble wording.
And al-Ḥuṭayʾa combined praise and satire in a single verse from a poem in which he praised Baghīḍ and satirised al-Zibriqān, and al-Zibriqān complained of him because of it to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb:
قد ناضلونا وسلوا من كنانتهم ... مجدا تليدا ونبلا غير أنكاس
(They contended with us and drew from their quiver an ancient glory and arrows that are not defective)
The meaning of this verse is known only to one who knows that the custom of the Arabs, when they bestowed a favour on a captive, was to give him arrows of theirs bearing a mark indicating that they belonged to those people and were still in his quiver. So al-Ḥuṭayʾa said to this man whom he meant by this praise: when your enemies vied with you in boasting, they drew from their quiver those very arrows which you had given them, until you bestowed favour on them, and these testify for you that they are your freed men; so this was an ancient glory of yours which they cannot deny, and it is proved for you by these arrows, which are not defective, meaning accurate ones that do not go astray when one shoots with them at the target. This is the utmost praise for the praised man and the extreme of satire against his enemies, since he reports that, despite knowing his favour to them, they boast against him with what, when they bring it out, establishes his superiority over them; and this is the extreme of ignorance and stupidity on their part.
Among the combinations of satire and praise or boasting is the saying of Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī:
بأي لسان ذامني متجاهل ... عليّ وخفق الريح فيّ ثناء
(With what tongue does a feigning ignorant man blame me, when the rustle of the wind about me is praise?)
تكلم بالقول المضلّل حاسد ... وكل كلام الحاسدين هراء
(An envier spoke misleading words, and all the talk of enviers is nonsense)
أتمشي القوافي تحت غير لوائنا ... ونحن على قوالها أمراء ولا سار في عرض السماوة بارق ... وليس له من قومنا خفراء
(Do verses march under a banner other than ours, when we are commanders over those who speak them? And no lightning has travelled across the breadth of the desert without guards from our people)
So when he boasts of himself he satirises his own kind, who vaunt themselves while being short, and claim knowledge while ignorance surrounds them. Did he not say to them, addressing them:
غدوت مريض العقل والدين فالقني ... لتخبر أبناء العقول الصحائح
(I became sick in intellect and religion; so meet me, that you may inform the sons of sound minds)
The ʿAlāʾī spirit is well known, so there is no need for explanation and elaboration.
As for combining congratulation and condolence, it is truly rare and requires much refinement of nature and delicacy of feeling to do it well. Among the most beautiful I have heard of it is the saying of the one offering condolences to Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya when he sat on the seat of the caliphate and delegations came to congratulate and to offer condolences for his father. When they had gathered, none was given the opening for speech that this speaker whose mention preceded was given, so he came forward and asked permission to speak, and when permitted he said: "May Allah reward you, O Commander of the Believers, for the calamity, and bless you in the gift. You have suffered a great loss and been given a great bestowal: you have lost the caliph of Allah, and been given the caliphate of Allah; so be patient over what you have lost and give thanks for what you have been given." And he recited:
اصبر يزيد فقد فارفت ذا ثقة ... واشكر حباء الذي بالملك أصفاكا
(Be patient, Yazīd, for you have parted from a trusted one, and give thanks for the gift of Him who has granted you kingship)
لا رزء أصبح في الأقوام تعلمه ... كما رزئت ولا عقبى كعقباكا
(There is no loss among the peoples you know of like the one you suffered, nor any outcome like your outcome)
أصبحت راعي أمور الناس كلهم ... فأنت ترعاهم والله يرعاكا وفي معاوية الباقي لنا خلف ... إذا نعيت ولا نسمع بمنعاكا
(You have become the guardian of the affairs of all the people; you tend them and Allah tends you; and in Muʿāwiya [who remains] we have a successor, when you are mourned, and may we not hear of your death-announcement)
[Translator's note: the source reads «فارفت»; presumably «فارقت».] He thereby opened for the people the door of speech, and they spoke, and he had the merit of precedence.
And Abū Nuwās said to al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Faḍl, consoling him for al-Rashīd and congratulating him on the caliphate of al-Amīn:
تعزّ أبا العباس عن خير هالك ... بأكرم حي كان أو هو كائن
(Take comfort, Abū al-ʿAbbās, for the best of the departed, with the noblest living man there ever was or will be)
حوادث أيام تدور صروفها ... لهنّ مساو مرة ومحاسن
(Events of days whose vicissitudes revolve; at times they have evils, at times good things)
وفي الحيّ بالميت الذي غيّب الثرى ... فلا أنت مغبون ولا الموت غابن
(And in the living one there is [compensation] for the dead whom the earth has hidden; so you are not cheated, nor is death the cheater)

3- The art of iltifāt (shift of address):
In His saying, Exalted is He: «وَإِنْ مِنْكُمْ إِلَّا وارِدُها ... الخ» there is an iltifāt according to one of the two views, which is based on intending generality in the first [address], so that those addressed first are those addressed second, except that the first address is in the wording of the third person and the second in the wording of the second person. But if we build on the view that the first was meant only for a specific group, then in both cases the second is not an iltifāt but a turning away from a specific address to certain people to an address to people in general. The discussion of the arrival at Hell is long and is referred to in the larger works.

* Benefits:
A long discussion about ayyuhum:
We promised you more discussion of ayyuhum in His saying, Exalted is He, «ثُمَّ لَنَنْزِعَنَّ مِنْ كُلِّ شِيعَةٍ أَيُّهُمْ أَشَدُّ عَلَى الرَّحْمنِ عِتِيًّا». Abū Ḥayyān said in his commentary on al-Tashīl: "Al-Kisāʾī asked in the circle of Yūnus why one may not say «أعجبني أيهم قام», and he said: 'Ayy was created thus'", that is, was set down thus. And Ibn al-Sarrāj, justifying al-Kisāʾī's prohibition, said what amounts to this: ayy was set down for generality and indefiniteness, so when you say «يعجبني أيهم يقوم» it is as though you said "I like the person from whom standing occurs, whoever he may be"; but if you said «أعجبني أيهم قام» it would apply only to the person who stood, which takes it out of the generality for which it was set down. Therefore it is stipulated that its governor be future and precede it, as in «لننزعن من كل شيعة أيهم أشد», in order to distinguish the conditional and interrogative from the relative, because the conditional and interrogative are governed only by what follows them. The well-known view among the majority is that it is singular and masculine, though it may be feminine, dual and plural according to some, so you say ayyatun, ayyāni, ayyatāni, ayyūna, ayyātun. It is declinable: it was said so absolutely, and that is the view of al-Khalīl, Yūnus, al-Akhfash, al-Zajjāj and the Kufans. Sībawayh said it is indeclinable on ḍamma when it is annexed in wording and the head of its ṣila is an omitted pronoun. Al-Zajjāj said, rejecting this: "It has not become clear to me that Sībawayh erred except in two places, this being one of them, for he concedes that it is declined when it is alone, so how can he say it is indeclinable when annexed?"
Those who prohibit [the relative reading] claimed that ayy in the verse is interrogative, that it is a mubtadaʾ and ashaddu its khabar. Then they differed over the object of nanziʿa: al-Khalīl said it is omitted and the implied form is "la-nanziʿanna those of whom it is said 'ayyuhum ashaddu'"; Yūnus said the object is the clause, and nanziʿa was suspended from governing it; al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash said the object is kulla shīʿatin and min is redundant. Ibn Hishām rejected all these statements, saying: their views are refuted by the fact that suspension (taʿlīq) is specific to verbs of the heart, that one may not say «لأضربن الفاسق» with nominative by implying "the one of whom it is said he is the wrongdoer", and that the redundancy of min in an affirmative context is not established.
We cite here what Abū al-Baqāʾ said, for its brevity and comprehensiveness. He said: "His saying «أيهم أشد» is read with accusative, irregularly, and its governor is «لننزعن», and it means 'alladhī'; and it is read with ḍamma, and there are two views on that. One is that it is a ḍamma of indeclinability, which is Sībawayh's doctrine, and it means 'alladhī'. It was made indeclinable here because its original state is indeclinability, as it means 'alladhī' and is among the relative nouns, except that it was declined by analogy with kull or baʿḍ; so when it is linked with a complete clause it remains declined, and when its returning pronoun is omitted it is indeclinable because of its difference from the remaining relatives, thus returning to its right of indeclinability by departing from its peers; and its position is accusative by removal of the preposition. The second view is that it is a ḍamma of declension, and there are five views on it. The first is that it is a mubtadaʾ and ashaddu its khabar, and it is by way of quotation, the implied form being 'la-nanziʿanna from every shīʿa the group of which it is said: ayyuhum'; on this it is interrogative; this is the view of al-Khalīl. The second is likewise in being a mubtadaʾ and khabar and interrogative, except that the position of the clause is accusative by nanziʿa, which is a verb suspended from governing, and its meaning is discernment, close to the meaning of knowing, which may be suspended, as in your saying 'ʿalimtu ayyuhum fī al-dāri'; this is the view of Yūnus. The third is that the clause is resumptive, ayy is interrogative and min is redundant, i.e. 'la-nanziʿanna kulla shīʿatin'; this is the view of al-Akhfash and al-Kisāʾī, both of whom allow redundant min in the affirmative. The fourth is that ayyuhum is nominative by shīʿa, because its meaning is 'tashayyaʿa', and the implied form is 'la-nanziʿanna from every group that follows, whichever of them is most severe', and on this it means 'alladhī'; this is the view of al-Mubarrad. The fifth is that nanziʿa was suspended from governing because the meaning of the speech is the meaning of a condition, and a condition does not govern what precedes it, the implied form being 'la-nanziʿannahum, whether they followed or did not follow', or 'if they followed'; similarly 'la-aḍribanna ayyuhum ghaḍiba', i.e. 'whether they were angry or not'; this is the view of Yaḥyā on the authority of al-Farrāʾ, and it is the furthest of them from correctness."

dervis-irab:41-50.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الصِّدِّيقُ): one of the patterns of intensification, with similar forms such as الضحيّك and النّطّيق. What is meant is that he was thoroughly truthful in his words and deeds, and in affirming the unseen realities of Allah the Exalted, His signs, His books and His messengers.
(مَلِيًّا): a long span of time.
(حَفِيًّا):
In al-Mukhtār: «ḥafiya bihi (with kasra on the fāʾ), ḥafāwatan (with fatḥa on the ḥāʾ): so he is ḥafī, that is, one who is lavish in honouring him, treating him kindly and attending to his affairs. Al-ḥafī also means the one who presses for detail in questioning.» The first sense is that of His saying: «إِنَّهُ كانَ بِي حَفِيًّا», and the second that of His saying: «كَأَنَّكَ حَفِيٌّ عَنْها».

* I'rab:
(وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتابِ إِبْراهِيمَ إِنَّهُ كانَ صِدِّيقاً نَبِيًّا): The wāw is resumptive. (اذكر) is an imperative verb, its agent a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you". (في الكتاب) is a pair attached to (اذكر) (preposition and its genitive noun). (ابراهيم) is a direct object. (إنّ) and its noun; the clause of (كان) is its predicate, and the noun of (كان) is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he". (صديقا) is the first predicate of (كان) and (نبيا) is its second predicate.
(إِذْ قالَ لِأَبِيهِ يا أَبَتِ لِمَ تَعْبُدُ ما لا يَسْمَعُ وَلا يُبْصِرُ وَلا يُغْنِي عَنْكَ شَيْئاً)
As for (إذ), the grammarians differ about it. Al-Zamakhsharī, Abu al-Baqa and others attached it to (كان) or to (صديقا نبيا), meaning: he combined the characteristics of the prophets and the truthful ones when he addressed his father with those words. This rests on the working of the deficient kāna and its sisters on an adverbial other than their predicate and noun, which is disputed. Al-Zamakhsharī, Abu al-Baqa and others also parsed it as a badal (substitute) for (ابراهيم), on the assumption of an omitted muḍāf, meaning "the account of Ibrahim"; the clause (إنه كان صديقا نبيا) would then be parenthetical. This too rests on (إذ) being used freely (as a noun), a matter already discussed, along with the view that it is not used so. The clause (قال) is the genitive complement of it (the adverb). (لأبيه) is a pair attached to (قال). (يا) is a vocative particle and (أبت) is the one addressed, a muḍāf to the speaker's yāʾ, which has been replaced by the tāʾ. This was pointed out earlier. It is not permissible to combine the replacement and the thing replaced, so one does not say يا أبتي, but one may say يا أبتا since the alif stands in place of the yāʾ. Sībawayh compared it to أينق (in which the yāʾ is a replacement for the omitted wāw). More on this will come in the section on Benefits, together with an extended biography of Sībawayh.
(لم) is originally the prepositional lām plus the interrogative (ما). It has already been explained that the alif of (ما) is dropped when a preposition precedes it, and the lām is treated with it as one word, so the alif is written as a yāʾ; thus you say إلام, علام and حتام. It and its genitive noun are attached to (تعبد). The agent of (تعبد) is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you". (ما) is a relative noun, a direct object; the clause (لا يسمع) is its ṣila (relative clause), and what follows is conjoined to it. (شيئا) is a direct object or a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object); its treatment has already been given.
(يا أَبَتِ إِنِّي قَدْ جاءَنِي مِنَ الْعِلْمِ ما لَمْ يَأْتِكَ فَاتَّبِعْنِي أَهْدِكَ صِراطاً سَوِيًّا)
(يا أبت): its parsing has been given. (إنّ) and its noun; the clause (قد جاءني) is its predicate. (من العلم) is a pair attached to (جاءني), and (من) is partitive. (ما) is a relative noun, an agent; the clause (لم يأتك) is the ṣila. (فاتبعني): the fāʾ is the "eloquent" fāʾ (al-fāʾ al-faṣīḥa), meaning "if you wish for guidance and salvation, then follow me". (اتبعني) is an imperative verb, its agent a latent pronoun, with a direct object. (أهدك) is the response to the request, and for that reason it is jussive; the kāf is a direct object. (صراطا) is a second direct object, or it is accusative by removal of the preposition; (سويا) is an adjective of (صراطا).
(يا أَبَتِ لا تَعْبُدِ الشَّيْطانَ إِنَّ الشَّيْطانَ كانَ لِلرَّحْمنِ عَصِيًّا)
(لا) is prohibitive. (تعبد) is an imperfect verb, jussive by the prohibitive (لا); the agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you". (الشيطان) is a direct object. (إنّ) and its noun; the clause (كان) is its predicate, and the noun of (كان) is latent. (للرحمن) is a pair attached to (عصيا), and (عصيا) is the predicate of (كان).
(يا أَبَتِ إِنِّي أَخافُ أَنْ يَمَسَّكَ عَذابٌ مِنَ الرَّحْمنِ فَتَكُونَ لِلشَّيْطانِ وَلِيًّا)
(إنّ) and its noun; the clause (أخاف) is its predicate. (أن يمسك) is an interpreted maṣdar, a direct object of (أخاف). (عذاب) is the agent of (يمسك), and (من الرحمن) is an adjective of (عذاب). (فتكون) is conjoined to (أن يمسك); the noun of (تكون) is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you". (للشيطان) is a pair attached to (وليا), and (وليا) is the predicate of (تكون). The meaning of (الولي) here is the close companion.
(قالَ: أَراغِبٌ أَنْتَ عَنْ آلِهَتِي يا إِبْراهِيمُ)
The hamza is for the interrogative of disapproval. (راغب) is a mubtadaʾ, and the beginning with it is justified by its reliance on the interrogative particle. (أنت) is an agent which takes the place of the khabar. Al-Zamakhsharī parsed it as a fronted khabar with (أنت) as a postponed mubtadaʾ, but there is no need for that given the existence of the rule, whose exposition will come in the section on Benefits, along with the discussions that go with it which astonish the minds. (يا) is a vocative particle and (إبراهيم) is a one addressed, a proper noun in the singular, indeclinable on the ḍamma.
(لَئِنْ لَمْ تَنْتَهِ لَأَرْجُمَنَّكَ وَاهْجُرْنِي مَلِيًّا)
The lām is the one preparing for an oath. (إن) is conditional, (لم) is a particle of negation, inversion and jussion. (تنته) is an imperfect verb, jussive by (لم). (لأرجمنك): the lām falls in the response to the oath, as is the rule when an oath and a condition are combined. (أرجمنك) is an imperfect verb, indeclinable on the fatḥa; the agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "I", and the kāf is a direct object. (واهجرني): the wāw is a conjunction. (اهجرني) is conjoined to an omitted clause according to those who forbid the conjoining of an imperative/performative sentence to a declarative one, the implied form being "so beware of me and leave me". But Sībawayh allows the conjoining of a declarative clause to a performative clause, so this implied form is not required. (مليا) is an adverb of time attached to (اهجرني); it is also said to be a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent of (اهجرني), meaning "safe and sound, so that no harm befalls you".
(قالَ سَلامٌ عَلَيْكَ سَأَسْتَغْفِرُ لَكَ رَبِّي إِنَّهُ كانَ بِي حَفِيًّا)
(سلام) is a mubtadaʾ, and the beginning with it is justified by the sense of supplication it carries; the supplication meant here is bidding farewell and resolving on separation. (عليك) is the khabar. (سأستغفر): the sīn is for the future. (أستغفر) is an imperfect verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "I". He was permitted to seek forgiveness for the unbeliever only out of the hope that he would be granted success to attain faith, which brings about forgiveness of sins. (لك) is a pair attached to (أستغفر). (ربي) is a direct object. The clause (إنه) is causal and has no grammatical position. (إنّ) and its noun; the clause (كان) is its predicate, and the noun of (كان) is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he". (حفيا) is its predicate, and (بي) is a pair attached to (حفيا).
(وَأَعْتَزِلُكُمْ وَما تَدْعُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ)
The wāw is a conjunction. (أعتزلكم) means "I leave you, departing from your land"; the agent is latent and the kāf is a direct object. (وما): the wāw is a conjunction, and (ما) may be a relative or a maṣdarī particle. In either case its position is accusative, conjoined to the kāf, or it is a mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment). The clause (تدعون) is the ṣila, and (من دون الله) is a ḥāl.
(وَأَدْعُوا رَبِّي عَسى أَلَّا أَكُونَ بِدُعاءِ رَبِّي شَقِيًّا)
(أدعو) is conjoined to (أعتزلكم); its agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "I". (ربي) is a direct object. (عسى) is a past verb, one of the verbs of hope; its noun is latent, and (أن) with what is in its sphere is the predicate. The noun of (أكون) is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "I". (بدعاء) is a pair attached to (شقيا). (ربي) is a muḍāf ilayhi to (دعاء), and (شقيا) is the predicate of (أكون).
(فَلَمَّا اعْتَزَلَهُمْ وَما يَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ وَهَبْنا لَهُ إِسْحاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ وَكُلًّا جَعَلْنا نَبِيًّا)
(لما) is a temporal adverb of time-point, or a connective. (اعتزلهم) is a past verb with a latent agent and a direct object. The parsing of (وما يعبدون من دون الله) has been given earlier, meaning: he left them in deed, going from Babylon to the Holy Land. The clause (وهبنا) has no grammatical position since it is the response to (لما). (له) is a pair attached to (وهبنا). (إسحق) is the direct object of (وهبنا), and (يعقوب) is conjoined to (إسحق). (كلا) is the first direct object of (جعلنا), and (نبيا) is the second direct object.
(وَوَهَبْنا لَهُمْ مِنْ رَحْمَتِنا وَجَعَلْنا لَهُمْ لِسانَ صِدْقٍ عَلِيًّا)
(ووهبنا) is conjoined to the first (وهبنا). (لهم) is a pair attached to (وهبنا), meaning for Ibrahim and his two sons. (من رحمتنا) is a pair also attached to (وهبنا). (وجعلنا) is conjoined to (وهبنا). (لهم) is in the position of the second object of (جعلنا), and (لسان صدق) is the first object. (عليا) is an adjective of (لسان); it means fair praise, as will come in the section on Rhetoric.

* Rhetoric:
1- The art of istidrāj (gradual drawing-in):
These verses reach the summit of eloquence and contain wonders that astonish the minds. The first to meet us is an art known as istidrāj. It rests on beguiling the person addressed, in which words take the place of deeds: the speaker keeps being gentle with the addressee, circling around him and softening him, until the addressee is at a loss, yields, and announces his surrender. It resembles the people of dialectic in speech, logic and philosophy, except that those deal in syllogistic fallacies, whereas the poet or writer in his istidrāj deals in rhetorical fallacies. Imam al-Zamakhsharī did well in analysing this art, though he did not name it, and analysed this passage wonderfully. Ḍiyāʾ al-Dīn Ibn al-Athīr, who drew out this art, wished to raid al-Zamakhsharī's passage, blew it up wholesale and attributed it to himself. We shall do al-Zamakhsharī justice against those who robbed him by quoting his passage in full, long as it is, for it is like something beautiful that never wearies.
«Look: when he wished to counsel and admonish his father about the grave error he was entangled in, and the odious conduct in which he disobeyed the command of the wise and stripped himself of the verdict of discernment, and the stupidity beyond which there is no stupidity, how he arranged his speech to him in the finest order and drove it along the most graceful course, with courtesy, gentleness, kindness, softness, fine manners and good character, taking guidance in that from the counsel of his Lord, Mighty and Exalted ... He first asked him for the reason for his error, with the question of one who warns him about his persistence and awakens him to his excess and extremity. For if the object of worship were alive, discerning, hearing, seeing, able to reward and punish, beneficial and harmful, yet merely one of the creatures, it would still make light of the intellect of whoever deemed it fit for worship and described it as lordship, and would record against him clear error and great wrong, even if it were the noblest of creatures and the highest in rank ... So what do you think of one who directs his worship to an inanimate object with neither sense nor awareness, which does not hear, O worshipper, your mention of it and your praise of it, and does not see the postures of your submission and humility before it, let alone suffice you by your asking it to ward off a trial so that it wards it off, or by a need arising for you so that it fulfils it? Then he followed with his call to the truth, gently and kindly. He did not label him with extreme ignorance nor himself with surpassing knowledge, but said: I have with me a portion of knowledge, something of it that you do not have, namely knowledge of guidance to the straight path, so do not disdain it. Suppose that you and I are on a journey, and I have knowledge of the way which you lack: follow me and I shall deliver you from going astray and being lost. Then, thirdly, he discouraged him and forbade him what he was doing, saying that Satan, who rebelled against your Lord the Most Merciful, from Whom come all the blessings you have, is your enemy who wants for you nothing but every ruin, disgrace and punishment, and is the enemy of your father Adam and of all your kind, and it is he who entangled you in this misguidance, commanded it and made it seem fair to you; so if you look closely, you are a worshipper of Satan. But Ibrahim, peace be upon him, because of his deep sincerity and the loftiness of his aspiration in devotion to the Lord, mentioned of Satan's two offences only the one that concerns the Lord of Might, namely his disobedience and arrogance, and did not turn to mention his enmity to Adam and his offspring, as if contemplation of the enormity of what he committed in that had flooded his mind and closed over his thought. Then, fourthly, he warned him of the evil end and of the liability and ruin that what he was in draws after it. Even this was not devoid of fine manners, since he did not state outright that punishment was due to him or that torment clung to him, but said: I fear that a punishment may touch you. He mentioned fear and touching, left the punishment indefinite, and made allegiance to Satan and entering the company of his followers and friends greater than the punishment. That is because the good pleasure of Allah is greater than the reward itself, and Allah the Exalted named it as the witness to the great triumph ... so likewise allegiance to Satan, which is opposed to the good pleasure of Allah, is greater and graver than the punishment itself. He opened each of the four counsels with the words «يا أبت», as a plea to him and an appeal for his tenderness ... The old man turned on him with the coarseness of disbelief and the harshness of obstinacy, and called him by his name; he did not answer his «يا أبت» with «يا بني». He put the khabar before the mubtadaʾ in his words «أراغب أنت» because it was the more important to him, and in it is a kind of astonishment and denunciation of Ibrahim's turning away from his gods.»
2- Majāz mursal (loose metaphor):
In His saying «وَجَعَلْنا لَهُمْ لِسانَ صِدْقٍ عَلِيًّا» there is a majāz mursal, from the use of the name of the instrument, namely the tongue, since it is the instrument of speech, while what is meant is what arises from it. So "tongue" is used for what is produced by the tongue, just as "hand" is used for what is given by the hand, namely a gift. It is a figurative usage whose relation is causality.

* Benefits:
1- The adjective as mubtadaʾ:
A descriptive word (waṣf) may be made nominative by being a mubtadaʾ if it does not agree with the noun it describes in dual or plural; it then needs no khabar, but is satisfied with an agent or deputy agent, which is nominative by it and takes the place of the khabar, on the condition that the descriptive word is preceded by a negation or an interrogative. The descriptive word is then in the position of a verb: it is not dualised, pluralised, qualified, diminutive or made definite. The waṣf includes the active participle, the passive participle, the assimilated adjective, the elative, and the relative adjective (nisba). There is no difference between its being derived, as in:
ما ناجح الكسولان and هل محبوب المجتهدون,
or a solid noun containing the sense of an adjective, as in هل صخر هذان المعاندان: (صخر) is a mubtadaʾ, and it is a solid noun in the sense of a descriptive word, because it means hard and harsh, and (هذان) is an agent of (صخر) which dispenses with a khabar. Likewise ما وحشي أخلاقك: (وحشي) is a mubtadaʾ, a solid noun containing the sense of an adjective since it is a relative noun, so it is in the sense of a passive participle, and (أخلاقك) is its deputy agent, which dispenses with the khabar. There is no difference between the negation and interrogative being by a particle or by something else, as in: ليس كسول ولداك, غير كسول أبناؤك and كيف سائر أخواك. The difference is that with (ليس) the descriptive word is its noun, and the nominative after it is nominative by it, taking the place of the khabar; while with (غير) the status of mubtadaʾ passes to it, the descriptive word is made genitive by annexation to it, and what comes after the descriptive word is nominative by it, taking the place of the khabar. By this the difficulty in the verse of Abu Nuwas is resolved:
غير مأسوف على زمن ... ينقضي بالهم والحزن
(Not to be regretted is a time that passes in worry and grief.)
(غير) is a mubtadaʾ with no khabar; rather, what is nominative by the word annexed to it dispenses with the khabar. That is because it carries the sense of negation, and the descriptive word after it is genitive in form but is in force nominative by mubtadaʾ-hood. That is, the nominative vowel on (غير) is the one this noun deserves originally, but since it was occupied with the genitive vowel owing to annexation, its originally due vowel as a mubtadaʾ was made as a loan. (على زمن) is in the position of nominative as deputy agent of (مأسوف), taking the place of the khabar. The clause (ينقضي بالهم والحزن) is an adjective of (زمن). Ibn Hisham cited this verse in Mughni al-Labib and cited two other analyses which you will see are extremely far-fetched, especially the third, whose weakness Ibn Hisham himself admitted; refer to them there. «[Translator's note: the source reads "ibn Hisham" with the lowercase/colloquial spelling "بن هشام" and "تصفه"; the latter appears to be a misprint, probably for "ضعفه" (its weakness).]»
If the descriptive word does not occur after a negation or interrogative, this usage is not permitted. One does not say مجتهد غلاماك; rather agreement is required, as in مجتهدان غلاماك, and then it is a fronted khabar and what follows is a postponed mubtadaʾ. The Kufans allowed it, since they did not require the descriptive word to rely on negation or interrogative, and cited as evidence his saying:
خبير بنو لهب فلا تك ملغيا ... مقالة لهبي إذا الطير مرت
(The Banu Lahb are expert, so do not disregard the word of a Lahbī when the birds pass.)
They parsed (بنو لهب) as the agent of (خبير) without its relying on a negation or interrogative. The Basrans excused the verse by saying that (خبير) is on the pattern faʿīl, and faʿīl is on the pattern of the verbal nouns such as ṣahīl and zaʾīr, and a verbal noun can be predicated of the singular, dual or plural; so it was given the ruling of what is on its pattern. It is on the lines of His saying the Exalted: «وَالْمَلائِكَةُ بَعْدَ ذلِكَ ظَهِيرٌ». Abu al-Tayyib sided with the Kufans because he was from Kufa and because he had a passion for vexing the grammarians, as we have pointed out more than once, and he said his delightful verse:
دع النفس تأخذ وسعها قبل بينها ... فمفترق جاران دارهما العمر
(Let the soul take its fill before its parting; for two neighbours whose abode is life are bound to part.)
(مفترق) is a mubtadaʾ and (جاران) is an agent which takes the place of the khabar. It is not permissible to say that (مفترقا) is a fronted khabar, because it would then have had to agree with his words (جاران).
The upshot is that when the descriptive word makes what follows it nominative, it has three cases:
1- Mubtadaʾ-hood is obligatory if it does not agree with what follows in dual and plural, as in أقائم أخواك.
2- Khabar-hood is obligatory if it agrees with what follows in dual and plural, as in أقائمان أخواك.
3- Both are permitted if it agrees with what follows in masculine and feminine, as in:
أقائم أخوك and أقائمة أختك.
The place where both are permitted holds only when no obstacle exists. Some scholars counted among the obstacles His saying «أراغب أنت عن آلهتي», so that mubtadaʾ-hood is the only option, because making it a khabar would require separation between it and its complement, namely the preposition and its genitive noun. Others rejected this, defending al-Zamakhsharī, by saying that «عن آلهتي» is another complement. As for al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn al-Hajib, they stipulated in principle that the nominative should be an overt noun, yet al-Zamakhsharī himself permitted parsing (أنت) as the agent of (راغب).
2- Back to «يا أبت»:
We spoke about the dialect forms in the vocative annexed to the speaker's yāʾ. As for the tāʾ in يا أبت and يا أمت, it is the tāʾ of feminisation, like the tāʾ in قائمة and امرأة. Sībawayh said:
I asked al-Khalīl about the tāʾ in «يا أبت لا تفعل» and «يا أمت», and he said: this tāʾ is like the hāʾ in خالة and عمة, meaning that it is for feminisation. What shows that it is for feminisation is that you say at pause يا أبه and يا أمه, replacing it with hāʾ at pause, like قاعد and قاعده, on the lines of خال and خاله, عم and عمه. This tāʾ came in as a kind of replacement for the yāʾ of annexation; the original is يا أبي and يا أمي, then the yāʾ was dropped, content with the kasra before it, and then the tāʾ entered as a replacement for it. For that reason the two are not combined, so one does not say يا أبتي or يا أمتي, lest the replacement and the thing replaced be combined. This tāʾ is not added to a word that has a feminine from its own stem; so if you were to say, for يا خالي and يا عمي, يا خالت and يا عمت, it would not be permitted, because it would be confused with the feminine. As for the tāʾ entering «الأم», there is no problem in it since it is feminine. And as for its entering «الأب», it is for the sense of intensification, as in راوية and علامة.

3- Who is Sībawayh:
The name of Sībawayh has recurred often, and we must take a quick look at the story of his life, because there is benefit in it, and because he left us, in the grammar of the Basrans, the Book that has lasted to this day. It was the comprehensive book of grammar, so that it was said of it: "the Qur'an of grammar".
He is Abu Bishr ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn Qanbar al-Ḥārithī, the attribution being to al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb, a Yemeni tribe, and this attribution is by clientship (walāʾ), for Sībawayh was Persian. As for his epithet Sībawayh, it came to prevail over him. It is a Persian compound word of the blended type, from sīb, meaning "apple", and bōy, meaning "smell", so it means "the smell of apples", according to the rule of descriptive compounds in Persian. He was so named for the sweetness of his smell, or for his beauty and good character. It is also said to be compounded of sīb and wayh, a sound-word. Some who know the Persian language mention that wayh in that language means "like" and "similar", so the meaning of the compound is "like the apple". Likewise Niftawayh: "like naphtha", and ʿAmrawayh: "like ʿAmr".

The ruling on "Sībawayh":
What is current on the tongues is Sībawayh with fatḥa on the bāʾ and wāw, and a kasra on the hāʾ. This is a common ruling for proper names ending in -wayh. In the Book there is the saying of Sībawayh:
«ʿAmrawayh, in their view, is like Ḥaḍramawt in that the end is joined to the first. ʿAmrawayh as a definite noun is in the kasra in the genitive, nominative and accusative cases, without tanwīn; and as an indefinite noun you say: هذا عمرويه آخر and رأيت عمرويه آخر.» You see that in the Book he confined himself to what was well known among people. It may also be pronounced Sībawayh with ḍamma on the bāʾ, fatḥa on the yāʾ and sukūn on the hāʾ, which is ascribed to the non-Arabs, who avoided the first form because wayh is a sound of lamentation.

His birth and upbringing:
Sībawayh was born in al-Bayḍāʾ in the district of Iṣṭakhr in Fars, to Persian parents. The date of his birth is not known with certainty. He moved to Basra and received learning there; it and Kufa were the two preeminent cities in the sciences of Arabic and religion. Nothing is known of his family except what is reported, that he died in the presence of his brother, and we do not know whether his family moved with him to Basra. We see no mention of his father, and we see Bashshār satirising him when his fame spread, saying:
ظللت تغني سادرا في مساءتي ... وأمك بالمصرين تعطي وتأخذ
(You went on singing, heedless, to my distress, while your mother in the two cities gives and takes.)
It appears from this that his mother was with him in Iraq. We do not know whether he married. In a report from al-Farrāʾ, Sībawayh had a female slave who served him, and in Ṭabaqāt al-Nuḥāh it is said that his slave-girl tore up the slips of his book, so he divorced her. Does he mean by his "slave-girl" his wife, or by "divorcing" her, putting her out of his house? It seems he had neither wife nor child, and the sign of that is that after he failed in Baghdad in his episode with al-Kisāʾī, as will come, he did not return to his home in Basra. «[Translator's note: the source reads «أم يعد»; the sense requires «لم يعد» ("did not return"), as translated.]»

How he took up grammar:
Sībawayh used to attend Ḥammād ibn Salama, the master of ḥadīth and transmission in Basra in his time. Ḥammād dictated the ḥadīth to him: «The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: There is none of my Companions but I have taken to task, except Abu al-Dardāʾ.» Sībawayh, who had picked up something of grammar, said: ليس أبو الدرداء (reading it as nominative). Ḥammād said: "You made a grammatical error, Sībawayh." Sībawayh said: "No doubt, I shall seek a knowledge in which you will never catch me in error." He turned to the study of grammar and attached himself to al-Khalīl. Sībawayh had thought that what follows ليس must be nominative so as to be its noun, not having known the construction of ليس in exception; Sībawayh addressed this in the Book and treated it fully in explanation and justification.

Early signs of his genius and his freedom of thought:
Most of what he received was from al-Khalīl, so that when he says "he said" or "I asked him", he means al-Khalīl. Al-Khalīl recognised his worth, the acuteness of his mind and the strength of his intelligence, so he imparted his knowledge to him and was sincere in teaching him. He also took from others than al-Khalīl: he took from ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb, and al-Akhfash the Elder Abu al-Khaṭṭāb ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn ʿAbd al-Majīd. Abu Zayd al-Anṣārī mentions that when Sībawayh says "the trustworthy one informed me", it is he whom he means. The first sign of his genius to appear was what al-Akhfash related. He said: I was with Yūnus when someone said to him, "Sībawayh has come." He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from him." He came and asked him, saying: How do you say:
مررت به المسكين?
He said: It is permissible to make it genitive as a badal from the hāʾ. (Sībawayh) said to him: And فمررت به المسكين with nominative, in the sense of "المسكين, I passed by him"? He said: That is wrong, because the pronoun comes before the overt noun. He said to him: Al-Khalīl allowed that and recited verses for it. He said: It is wrong. He said: And فمررت به المسكين with accusative? He said: Permissible. He said: On what basis? He said: As a ḥāl. He said: Did you not tell me that a ḥāl is not with the article (al-)? He said: You are right. Then he said to Sībawayh: What did your master say about it, meaning al-Khalīl? Sībawayh said: He said it is accusative as an expression of compassion. He said: How fine that is. I saw him grieved at his own saying "I made it accusative as a ḥāl". Sībawayh, with all his reverence for al-Khalīl, would also fault his words. In the Book: «Al-Khalīl claimed that a man may say: هذا رجل أخو زيد when you intend to liken him to the brother of Zayd. This is ugly and not permitted except where necessity compels. Were it permitted you would say هذا قصير الطويل, meaning like al-Ṭawīl, and that is not permitted, just as it is ugly for a definite noun to be a ḥāl like an indefinite one except in poetry.»

Between Sībawayh and al-Kisāʾī:
Fortune and good luck came to al-Kisāʾī and his companions, and they took a high station in Baghdad. Among them were the tutors of the caliphs' children, though in grammar and letters they were, in the Basrans' view, less learned and weaker in means. Sībawayh, the imam of the Basrans, thought to contest them in their position, so he made for Baghdad and proposed to the Barmakids that they bring him and al-Kisāʾī together to debate him, confident that he would have success and victory. News of Sībawayh's arrival reached al-Kisāʾī, who feared the consequence of the debate, that his authority in Baghdad might vanish. He went to Jaʿfar ibn Yaḥyā ibn Barmak and to al-Faḍl his brother and said: I am your friend and your associate, and this man has only come to remove my station. They said: Then take care for yourself, for we shall bring you together. It seems that Sībawayh's Persian descent was matched by al-Kisāʾī's, for he too was Persian, a descendant of Bahman ibn Fayrūz, and an Asadī by clientship; so Sībawayh had nothing that made him closer to the hearts of the Barmakids than al-Kisāʾī. He and his companions devised a plan, and it turned out as they expected: his companions would come ahead of him to the debating session and ask Sībawayh questions and gang up on him in them, until, when his zeal had cooled and his fatigue was plain, al-Kisāʾī would come and find an opponent whose edge had gone dull and whose vigour had gone, and he would get what he wanted, throwing him down. The story of the Hornet question (al-masʾala al-zunbūriyya) has been given in another place in this book.

dervis-irab:16-21.t:
* Vocabulary:
(انْتَبَذَتْ): al-intibādh is withdrawal and solitude. Mary withdrew for worship to a place on the eastern side of Bayt al-Maqdis, or from her house, secluded from the people [Translator's note: the source repeats "الناس" twice here]; other things were also said, and the details are in the longer works. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "intabadhat makānan: she took a place apart, far from the people."
(بَغِيًّا): al-baghy is the dissolute woman who seeks men. According to al-Mubarrad it is of the pattern faʿūl, that is, baghūy, and the wāw was assimilated into the yāʾ. Ibn Jinnī said in Kitāb al-Tamām: "It is of the pattern faʿīl; had it been faʿūl it would have been said baghūw, as it is said 'so-and-so is nahūw ʿan al-munkar' (a great forbidder of evil)." One says baghat fulāna bighāʾan (with kasra on the bāʾ), and from it slave women were called al-baghāyā, because they used to commit prostitution in the Jāhiliyya. One says: "al-baghāyā stood over their heads." Al-Aʿshā said:
والبغايا يركضن أكسية الاضر ... يج والشرعبيّ ذا الأذيال
(And the harlots trail the cloaks of al-Aḍrīj and the long-skirted Sharʿabī.)
In al-Qāmūs and its commentary: "baghā yabghī (of the pattern ḍaraba) al-shayʾa bighāʾan (with ḍamma on the bāʾ) and baghyan (with fatḥa) and bughā'an and bughyatan: he sought it. Baghā al-rajul: the man turned away from the truth and disobeyed. Baghā ʿalayhi: he exalted himself over him and wronged him, so he is bāghin." Perhaps their applying the word bighāʾ to lewdness and fornication is taken from this meaning, because it is among the motives of what the people of obscenity and depravity seek.

* I'rab:
(وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتابِ مَرْيَمَ إِذِ انْتَبَذَتْ مِنْ أَهْلِها مَكاناً شَرْقِيًّا)
واذكر: the wāw is resumptive, and اذكر is an imperative verb with a latent agent, its implied form being "you". في الكتاب is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to اذكر. مريم is a direct object. As for إذ, Abū al-Baqāʾ said, verbatim: "In إذ there are four possibilities. The first is that it is an adverbial, and the governing element in it is omitted, its implied form being 'and mention the account of Mary when she withdrew'. The second is that it is a ḥāl from an omitted muḍāf. The third is that it is made accusative by an omitted verb, that is, 'and make clear when she withdrew', so it belongs to another sentence, as Sībawayh said about his saying, the Exalted, «انْتَهُوا خَيْراً لَكُمْ»; it is stronger as an adverbial, even if it is a direct object. The fourth is that it is a substitute for Mary, a badal ishtimāl, because times include persons; al-Zamakhsharī mentioned it, and it is far-fetched, because time, when it is not a ḥāl of the person, nor a predicate of it, nor a description of it, cannot be a substitute for it. It was also said that إذ has the sense of the maṣdar أن, as in your saying 'I will not honour you since you did not honour me', that is, 'because you did not honour me'. On this basis badal ishtimāl is sound: 'and mention Mary's withdrawing.'"
Ibn Hishām's statements about it are inconsistent. While he says in his discussion of إذ: "The third use is that it be a substitute for the object, as in «وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتابِ مَرْيَمَ إِذِ انْتَبَذَتْ»; so إذ is a badal ishtimāl from مريم, on the lines of the substitute in «يسألونك عن الشهر الحرام قتال فيه»", he then returns and says: "The majority claimed that إذ occurs only as an adverbial or as annexed to, and that in such as «واذكروا إذ كنتم قليلا» it is an adverbial for an omitted object, that is, 'remember the favour of Allah when you were few', and in such as إذ انتبذت it is an adverbial for a muḍāf to an omitted object, that is, 'and mention the story of Mary'."
Shihāb al-Dīn al-Ḥalabī, known as al-Samīn, said: "In إذ there are several possibilities. The first is that it is accusative by اذكر, having left the sense of the adverbial, since it is impossible for it to remain in its past sense while that which governs it is explicit as to futurity. The second is that it is accusative by an omitted element annexed to Mary, its implied form being 'and mention the report of Mary, or her tidings, when she withdrew', so إذ is made accusative by that report or tidings. The third is that it is a badal ishtimāl from Mary. Al-Zamakhsharī said: 'because times include what is in them, for what is meant by mentioning Mary is the mention of her time, because this wondrous story took place in it.'" The clause انتبذت is annexed to إذ. من أهلها is a ḥāl. مكانا is an adverbial attached to انتبذت, that is, "in a place". شرقيا is an adjective. It is also permissible to parse مكانا as a direct object, on the basis that انتبذت means "she came to"; the text of al-Miṣbāḥ supports its being a direct object, so consider that in the section on vocabulary. (فَاتَّخَذَتْ مِنْ دُونِهِمْ حِجاباً فَأَرْسَلْنا إِلَيْها رُوحَنا فَتَمَثَّلَ لَها بَشَراً سَوِيًّا)
The fāʾ is a conjunction. اتخذت is a past verb with a latent agent. من دونهم is a second direct object and حجابا is the first direct object. فأرسلنا is conjoined to فاتخذت. إليها is attached to أرسلنا, and روحنا is a direct object. فتمثل is likewise a conjunction. لها is attached to تمثل. بشرا is a ḥāl, and سويا is an adjective; its description is what allows a rigid noun to occur as a ḥāl, and more discussion of this will come in the section on benefits. (قالَتْ: إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِالرَّحْمنِ مِنْكَ إِنْ كُنْتَ تَقِيًّا)
إن and its noun, and the clause أعوذ is its khabar, and the sentence is the content of the saying. بالرحمن is attached to أعوذ, and منك is also attached to أعوذ. إن is a conditional, jussive-making particle. كنت is a defective past verb, and the tāʾ is its noun, and تقيا is its khabar. The apodosis is omitted, and the meaning is: "If it is hoped of you that you fear Allah, dread Him and heed seeking refuge in Him, then I take refuge in Him from you." (قالَ إِنَّما أَنَا رَسُولُ رَبِّكِ لِأَهَبَ لَكِ غُلاماً زَكِيًّا)
إنما is a restraining particle together with what it restrains. أنا is a mubtadaʾ and رسول ربك is the khabar. The lām is for cause, and أهب is an imperfect verb made accusative by an implied أن after the lām. لك is attached to أهب. غلاما is a direct object and زكيا an adjective. (قالَتْ: أَنَّى يَكُونُ لِي غُلامٌ وَلَمْ يَمْسَسْنِي بَشَرٌ وَلَمْ أَكُ بَغِيًّا)
أنى is an interrogative noun meaning "how", and its parsing has been given earlier in the story of Zechariah. ولم يمسسني: the wāw is circumstantial, لم is a particle of negation, reversal and jussive, and يمسسني is an imperfect verb made jussive by لم, the yāʾ being a direct object and بشر the agent. ولم أك بغيا: لم is a particle of negation, reversal and jussive; أك is an imperfect verb in the jussive, its sign of jussive being sukūn on the nūn, which was omitted for lightness; the noun of أك is latent; and بغيا is its khabar. (قالَ كَذلِكِ قالَ رَبُّكِ هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ): كذلك is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, and the parsing of its like has been given earlier. (وَلِنَجْعَلَهُ آيَةً لِلنَّاسِ وَرَحْمَةً مِنَّا وَكانَ أَمْراً مَقْضِيًّا): لنجعله is a cause whose thing caused is omitted, that is, "We did that"; or it is conjoined to an implied element, that is, "so as to show by it Our power and to make him a sign". آية is a second direct object of لنجعله, and للناس is an adjective of آية. رحمة منا is conjoined to آية. وكان أمرا مقضيا: كان and its latent noun and its khabar, and مقضيا is an adjective.

* Benefits:
The meaning of «بشرا سويا»:
The discussion of the ḥāl muwaṭṭiʾa (preparatory circumstantial) has been given earlier: it is a rigid noun that is described, and this is one of its conditions that justify its being rigid. In the verse it is بشرا, which is a ḥāl from the agent of تمثل, namely the angel, and reliance in it is on the adjective, which is سويا, a derived noun, because it is a resembling adjective (ṣifa mushabbaha). The wording of Ibn Hishām: "The second: its division, according to whether it is intended for itself or for preparation by it, into two kinds: the intended, which is the usual, and the preparatory, which is the rigid described one, as in «فَتَمَثَّلَ لَها بَشَراً سَوِيًّا»."
Some objected to this parsing and said: the claim of ḥāl requires that the meaning be "he appeared to her in the state of her being a human", and it is not hidden that at the time of appearing he was an angel, not a human; so the nearer view is that it is accusative by removal of the preposition, that is, "he appeared to her as a human", meaning that he took his likeness and was formed in his shape.
Know that al-Bayḍāwī said here something unseemly, where he said: "Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to her in the form of a beardless youth, perfectly formed, so that she might be comforted by his speech, and perhaps to stir her desire so that her seed would descend into her womb." His saying "to stir" etc. is a wording unfitting for Mary, given the verified fact that Jesus, peace be upon him, belonged to the world of the Command (ʿālam al-amr), that is, the command of creation, exemplified by the saying of the Exalted: «إِنَّما قَوْلُنا لِشَيْءٍ إِذا أَرَدْناهُ أَنْ نَقُولَ لَهُ كُنْ فَيَكُونُ», for there is there no saying, nor "was", nor "will be". And this is the aspect of likeness between Jesus and Adam in the saying of the Exalted: «إِنَّ مَثَلَ عِيسى عِنْدَ اللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ آدَمَ», that is, in creation by the Command without intermediary or seed. The blowing indicated by the saying of the Exalted «فَنَفَخْنا فِيهِ مِنْ رُوحِنا» is of the kind of parable, borrowed for the pouring out of that by which there is actual life upon matter capable of receiving it; not the reality of blowing, which is the passage of wind into a cavity fit to retain it and be filled by it.
It is not sound to excuse al-Qāḍī al-Bayḍāwī on the ground that he looked to the divine custom of creating effects after causes, because the cause must be complete, and the woman's seed alone is not a complete cause for the conception of a child. He appeared to her in a beautiful form only that she might be comforted by him and not recoil from him, but listen to him and prick up her ears to hear the glad tidings; and it was in the form of a beardless youth because of women's familiarity with children and with those who are near them, and the absence of reserve with them. As for the account of al-Zamakhsharī, it is: "It was said that she sat in an elevated place to wash from menstruation, screened by a wall or something that covered her. Her place was the mosque; when she menstruated she moved to her maternal aunt's house, and when she became pure she returned to the mosque. While she was in her place of washing the angel came to her in the form of a young man, radiant of face, with curly hair, perfectly formed, nothing lacking from the human form; or beautiful in form and well-proportioned. He appeared to her in the form of a human only so that she might be comforted by his speech and not recoil from him; had he appeared to her in angelic form she would have recoiled and been unable to listen to his words." Al-Zamakhsharī continued his speech and said: "It indicates her chastity and piety that she sought refuge in Allah from that beautiful form of surpassing beauty; his appearing in that description was a trial for her and a test of her chastity. It was also said: she was in the house of the husband of her sister, Zechariah, and she had a private sanctuary (miḥrāb) in which she lived; when Zechariah went out he locked the door on her. She wished to find a solitary place on the mountain to delouse her head, and the roof split open for her, so she went out and sat in the elevated place behind the mountain, and the angel came to her."
We conclude this section, in which we departed from the condition of our book because of its importance, with an appendix by Shaykh ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Kāshī, and this is his text: "He appeared to her as a well-formed human, beautiful in form, so that her soul would be affected by him and be moved according to the natural disposition, or the effect would pass from the imagination into the nature and her desire would be moved and she would emit, as happens in sleep with a wet dream. The generation of a child from a single seed was possible because it is established in the natural sciences that the male's fluid in the generation of the foetus is in the position of rennet in cheese, and the female's fluid in the position of milk: that is, the coagulating comes from the male's fluid and the coagulating-into from the female's fluid, not in the sense that the male's fluid alone has the coagulating power and the female's alone the coagulable power, but in the sense that the coagulating power in the male's fluid is stronger; otherwise it would not be possible for them to become one thing, nor would the male's fluid coagulate so as to become part of the child. On this basis, if the female's temperament is strong and masculine, as are the temperaments of noble-souled women of strong faculties, and the temperament of her liver is hot, the fluid that separates from her right kidney is much hotter than the fluid that separates from her left kidney; so when the two meet in the womb, and the temperament of the womb is strong in retention and attraction, what separates from the right kidney takes the place of the man's fluid in the strength of the coagulating power, and what separates from the left kidney takes the place of the female's fluid in the strength of coagulability, and so the child is created. This holds especially when the soul is supported by the Holy Spirit and strengthened by it: the effect of its connection with it passes into the nature and the body and changes the temperament and supplies all the faculties in their actions with spiritual aid, so that she becomes more capable of her actions in ways that cannot be measured by analogy."

dervis-irab:51-58.t:
* I'rab:
(وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتابِ مُوسى إِنَّهُ كانَ مُخْلَصاً وَكانَ رَسُولًا نَبِيًّا): (اذكر) is an imperative verb. (في الكتاب) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (اذكر). (موسى) is a direct object. (إنّ) and its noun; the clause (كان) is its predicate. (مخلصا) is the predicate of (كان). (وكان رسولا نبيا) is conjoined to the first (كان).
(وَنادَيْناهُ مِنْ جانِبِ الطُّورِ الْأَيْمَنِ وَقَرَّبْناهُ نَجِيًّا): (وناديناه) is conjoined to what preceded; it is a verb, an agent and a direct object. (من جانب) is a pair attached to (ناديناه). (الطور) is a muḍāf ilayhi. (الأيمن) is an adjective of (جانب); they said it is so called because it was on the right of Musa when he came from Madyan. (وقربناه) is conjoined to (ناديناه). (نجيا) is a ḥāl from one of the two pronouns in (ناديناه) or (قربناه); it is faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil, that is, "one conversing in confidence".
(وَوَهَبْنا لَهُ مِنْ رَحْمَتِنا أَخاهُ هارُونَ نَبِيًّا): (ووهبنا) is likewise a conjunction. (له) is a pair attached to (وهبنا). (من رحمتنا) is a pair also attached to (وهبنا). The meaning of (من) here is partitive, that is, "part of Our mercy", or causal, that is, "on account of Our mercy". (أخاه) is the direct object of (وهبنا), (هارون) is a badal, and (نبيا) is a ḥāl.
(وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتابِ إِسْماعِيلَ إِنَّهُ كانَ صادِقَ الْوَعْدِ وَكانَ رَسُولًا نَبِيًّا): Its parsing is evident and has been given. The clause (إنه كان) is causal.
(وَكانَ يَأْمُرُ أَهْلَهُ بِالصَّلاةِ وَالزَّكاةِ وَكانَ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِ مَرْضِيًّا): The clause (يأمر) is the predicate of (كان). (أهله) is a direct object. (بالصلاة) is a pair attached to (يأمر). (كان) is a deficient past verb whose noun is latent, its implied form being "he". (عند ربه) is a pair attached to (مرضيا), and (مرضيا) is the predicate of (كان). The wāw and the yāʾ came together, so the wāw was turned into yāʾ and merged into the other.
(وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتابِ إِدْرِيسَ إِنَّهُ كانَ صِدِّيقاً نَبِيًّا): The parsing of its like has been given. There is no harm in citing what al-Zamakhsharī said regarding Idris, and this is his text:
«It is said that he was named Idris for his much study (dars) of the Book of Allah, Mighty and Exalted, and that his name was Akhnūkh. This is not correct, because if it were ifʿīl from dars, it would have only one cause (of diptosy), namely being a proper name, and so would be fully declinable; its being diptote is therefore evidence that it is non-Arabic. Likewise Iblis is non-Arabic and not from iblās (despair), as they claim; nor is Yaʿqūb from ʿaqib (heel/offspring), nor Isrāʾīl "Isrāl" as Ibn al-Sikkīt claimed. Whoever has not verified and trained in the craft produces many such slips. It is possible that the meaning of Idris in that language is close to that, and the narrator reckoned it derived from dars.» How fine is freedom of opinion!
(وَرَفَعْناهُ مَكاناً عَلِيًّا): (رفعناه) is a verb, an agent and a direct object. (مكانا) is an adverbial attached to (رفعناه) and (عليا) is an adjective. Many legends have been related about this raising; their place is the longer works.
(أُولئِكَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ مِنَ النَّبِيِّينَ مِنْ ذُرِّيَّةِ آدَمَ): (أولئك) is a mubtadaʾ, meaning the ten prophets mentioned in the surah. (الذين) is the khabar or a badal from the demonstrative. The clause (أنعم الله عليهم) is the ṣila. (من النبيين) is a ḥāl. (من ذرية آدم) is a badal with repetition of the preposition.
(وَمِمَّنْ حَمَلْنا مَعَ نُوحٍ وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّةِ إِبْراهِيمَ وَإِسْرائِيلَ وَمِمَّنْ هَدَيْنا وَاجْتَبَيْنا): Conjoined to what preceded.
(إِذا تُتْلى عَلَيْهِمْ آياتُ الرَّحْمنِ خَرُّوا سُجَّداً وَبُكِيًّا): The clause (إذا تتلى عليهم) and its response is resumptive with no grammatical position if we parse (الذين) as a khabar; and if we parse (الذين) as a badal, then it is the khabar. The clause (خرّوا) has no grammatical position since it is the response to (إذا). The wāw in (خروا) is an agent. (سجدا) is a ḥāl from the agent, and (بكيا) is conjoined to (سجدا). Both are plurals of sājid and bākin; the second is irregular, because the regular rule for a fāʿil from a defective root is that it be pluralised on fuʿala, as qāḍin with plural quḍāt, and bākin with plural bukāt. «[Translator's note: the source writes the pattern as «فعله» and the plural of بالك as «بكاة»; I have given the regular pluralisation pattern as the text intends it. The source's spelling of the first pattern is rendered as fuʿala.]»

dervis-irab:59-63.t:
* Vocabulary:
(خلف): that is, a successor generation. Some lexicographers use al-khalf with sukūn on the lām, as here, for evil, so one says khalf sūʾ, and with fatḥa for good, so one says khalaf ṣāliḥ. In al-Kashshāf: «khalafahu when he succeeded him; then in the succession of good it was said khalaf with fatḥa, and in the succession of evil khalf with sukūn, as they said waʿd for the guarantee of good and waʿīd for the guarantee of evil.» Al-Liḥyānī said: al-khalaf with two fatḥas is the righteous child, and al-khalf with fatḥa and sukūn is the bad one.
(غَيًّا): every evil is ghayy among the Arabs and every good is rashād (right guidance). Al-al-Murāqqish al-Asghar said:
أمن حلم أصبحت تنكت واجما ... وقد تعتري الأحلام من كان نائما
فمن يلق خيرا يحمد الناس أمره ... ومن يغو لا يعدم على الغيّ لائما
(Is it from a dream that you have woken up, scratching the ground, dumbstruck? Dreams do visit one who is asleep. Whoever meets with good, people praise his affair; and whoever goes astray will not lack someone to blame him for the error.)
One says ghawiya, yaghwā (of the pattern daraba): he was immersed in ignorance.

* I'rab:
(فَخَلَفَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِمْ خَلْفٌ أَضاعُوا الصَّلاةَ وَاتَّبَعُوا الشَّهَواتِ فَسَوْفَ يَلْقَوْنَ غَيًّا): The fāʾ is a conjunction. (خلف) is a past verb. (من بعدهم) is a ḥāl. (خلف) is an agent. The clause (أضاعوا الصلاة) is an adjective of (خلف). (واتبعوا الشهوات) is conjoined to (أضاعوا الصلاة). The fāʾ is the "eloquent" fāʾ, meaning "if you wish to know their end". (سوف) is a particle of the future. (يلقون) is an imperfect verb and an agent, and (غيا) is a direct object.
(إِلَّا مَنْ تابَ وَآمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صالِحاً فَأُولئِكَ يَدْخُلُونَ الْجَنَّةَ وَلا يُظْلَمُونَ شَيْئاً): (إلا) is a particle of exception, and (من): if we make the exception discontinuous (munqaṭiʿ), (إلا) is in the sense of "but" and (من) is an excepted noun that must be accusative. The ground for discontinuity is that the excepted-from are unbelievers and the excepted are believers; this is the choice of al-Zajjāj. Abū Ḥayyān preferred continuity, which is perhaps the clearer, because it is an address suited to every community, among whom are those who believed and those who disbelieved. In either case it must be accusative, because the sentence is complete and affirmative. The clause (تاب) is the ṣila, (آمن) is conjoined to (تاب), and (عمل) is likewise conjoined. (صالحا) may be a direct object or a mafʿūl muṭlaq, that is, "righteous work". (فأولئك): the fāʾ is the "eloquent" fāʾ, and (أولئك) is a mubtadaʾ; the clause (يدخلون) is the khabar, and (الجنة) is a direct object by extension (ʿalā al-ittisāʿ). (ولا يظلمون) is conjoined to (يدخلون), and (شيئا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq; you may also make it a second object by giving (يظلمون) the sense of "they are diminished".
(جَنَّاتِ عَدْنٍ الَّتِي وَعَدَ الرَّحْمنُ عِبادَهُ بِالْغَيْبِ): (جنات) is a badal from (الجنة). (عدن) is a muḍāf ilayhi, from ʿadana bi-l-makān, meaning "he stayed in the place"; it has come to be used like a proper name, and for that reason it is permissible to qualify it with (التي). (التي) is an adjective of (جنات عدن). The clause (وعد) is the ṣila, (الرحمن) is the agent of (وعد), and (عباده) is the object. (بالغيب) is a ḥāl from (عباده), that is, from the object, the meaning being "unseen by them; they do not witness it". It may also be a ḥāl from the pronoun for the Garden, which is the pronoun returning to the relative noun, that is, "He promised it while they are absent from it, not seeing it".
(إِنَّهُ كانَ وَعْدُهُ مَأْتِيًّا): (إنّ) and its noun; the pronoun refers to Allah the Exalted, that is, al-Raḥmān, the meaning being that al-Raḥmān's promise is sure to be fulfilled; or it is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), because it is a setting of magnification and glorification. The clause is causal and resumptive. The clause (كان) is the predicate of (إنّ), and the noun of (كان) also refers to Allah the Exalted, with (وعده) a badal of that pronoun (badal al-ishtimāl), and (مأتيا) its predicate. It is also possible that there is no pronoun in it, with (وعده) its noun and (مأتيا) its predicate. Al-Jalāl and his commentators preferred that (مأتيا) is a passive form in the sense of an active, that is, "coming"; al-Zamakhsharī did not accept this, saying: «It is said that (مأتيا) is maf ʿūl in the sense of fāʿil, but the better view is that the promise is the Garden, and they come to it.» The truth is with al-Zamakhsharī, because what you come to also comes to you, so there is no need for reinterpretation.
(لا يَسْمَعُونَ فِيها لَغْواً إِلَّا سَلاماً وَلَهُمْ رِزْقُهُمْ فِيها بُكْرَةً وَعَشِيًّا): The clause is a ḥāl from (جنات عدن).
